title: Why Do We Dread Mondays?
content:
Why Do We Dread Mondays?

 

Every Monday, I struggle to wake up. I sleep through my alarms in the morning and then stagger to the bathroom with a sinking feeling in my stomach. Getting ready for the day seems more exhaustive than usual, and all I want to do is crawl back into my cozy bed. I resist the urge, make coffee, and steel my nerves for going to work. As I start my car and begin my commute, the sinking feeling in my stomach gets worse. It feels like I have a rock in my stomach that is slowly expanding, making me uncomfortable and gluing me to the fabric of my car seat. When I actually get to work and settle at my desk, I let out a heavy sigh and reluctantly sign onto my computer. I check emails, fumble through a crossword, procrastinate. It’s not a good start to my week, but it seems to consistently happen anyway.

 

A lot of people dread Mondays. It feels like a societal standard that we can’t escape, something that just comes with the working life. Stress surrounding starting a new week and especially going to work are at the forefront of Mondays, it’s our initial association with that time of the week. It’s so incredibly normalized that most people don’t even question it, but do we need to dread Mondays? It seems like a bad way to start the week, but what if it’s secretly productive in some way? Why do we actually dread Mondays?

 

For most people, a case of Monday dread actually stems from what some call the Sunday Scaries, an onset of dread or anxiety surrounding the idea of Monday. This often stems from being overstimulated or close to burnout at work. Productivity is incredibly valued right now, even sometimes over one’s own mental well-being. People in the workforce often work right on the edge of the point of burnout, working right up to that ledge can be incredibly exhausting. In addition to this, having a job where you are in a highly stimulating environment all day can cause mental exhaustion, leading to a negative association with that place of work.

 

Monday dread means that most employees feel less satisfaction and more stress with their jobs at the beginning of the week. It seems simple to point out, but this may be a sign that you don’t love your job, or it isn’t as fulfilling to you as it should be. Monday dread can be a sign that your workplace is putting you under various different stressors, which can cause a negative association to be formed. It can also be a sign that you feel misaligned with your position at work since the beginning of a new week can act as a reminder of your aimlessness. If you’re experiencing Monday dread, it might be worth looking into your relationship with your job.

 

Another common cause of dreading Mondays is having a packed or disruptive weekend schedule. It’s easy to want to catch up on sleep during the weekend, but studies show that drastically changing your sleep schedule is detrimental to the body. It also disrupts your natural bodily schedule. On the other side, over-packing your weekend can lead to a compound of fatigue from just doing too much. Letting loose and partying can be a great way to relax and be fun in the moment, but it definitely leaves a lasting impact on your energy levels. Having this kind of emphasis on weekends can mean that Mondays are a big emotional shift for some, leading to Monday dread.

 

Weekends are fun and work is not. Many people dread Mondays simply because they don’t feel free at work. Weekends often feel like a space of freedom and opportunity, whereas work feels like a place of constraint and stress. It’s hard to give up leisure and self-care for productivity, and most people simply don’t want to. It represents having to give up your time, instead of spending it in a way that you choose. If this is you, it may be time to reconsider your job and how comfortable you feel there. Feelings of steep change between the work week and weekend may indicate that you feel like you’re living a double life where you can’t be yourself at work.

 

Dreading Mondays is a normal part of life, but it can be an indicator of a larger sense of unhappiness. Work-life balance is an incredibly delicate thing to maintain, and sometimes you need some Monday dread to let you know your balance may be off. If you start your week already tired, you may need to reassess how you spend your weekends. The important thing is to be in touch with yourself and make sure to prioritize your mental health.

Stress surrounding starting a new week and especially going to work are at the forefront of Mondays, it’s our initial association with that time of the week. Why do we actually dread Mondays?

title: Examining Wellness Culture
content:
Examining Wellness Culture


Chasing wellness can give you something new to strive for, a better you. It’s easy to fall into a pattern of seeing impressive people on social media promoting a new tea or a new diet and jumping on the train. It’s a rat race of trying to better yourself through new things, all at the risk of being unhealthy. A wellness culture can be beneficial for making a community and better managing your health, but it can very easily become a toxic obsession. Can wellness culture ever make people feel good about themselves? Let’s take a deeper look.

 

Wellness culture always leaves you wanting more. It’s as if you’ll never be fully healthy without pursuing the newest health trend that’s being promoted online. It’s an insatiable need, the idea that you can always be doing more to be healthier. There is a kind of fear factor that is underlined throughout wellness culture as a whole. If you stop drinking bone broth for breakfast or skip a day of 5 am yoga, you’ll ruin your health completely. One step forward and fifty steps back, people are worried about having to start over completely if they mess up once. There are multiple threats presented, but the common ones I’ve noticed are illness and gaining weight. People are convinced that if they fall off of the health trend, they’ll develop chronic illness. Additionally to this, there is an underlying theme of fatphobia within the wellness community. We often see health influencers who are stick thin advertising their minimal diet and extensive workout routine. This can plant an idea that thin means healthy, which just is not true. Even so, this idea of what kind of bodies look healthy creates a weakness in consumers. You have to participate to look like this influencer. It can quickly become a game of guilt and shame, rather than one of empowerment and shared journeys. There is an endless push to keep consuming content and control every aspect of your health, which simply isn’t possible.

 

How many celebrities do you see on Instagram promoting a new laxative tea or gym clothing? I know for me, it’s a lot. It’s almost unavoidable, it feels like every other post on a celebrity’s feed is sponsored. This kind of product advertisement isn’t solely for the good health of their followers, there is a steep monetary gain involved. This can be through sponsorships (think #ad) or simply by gaining traction online. Outrageous lifestyles, especially those marketed as healthy, garner attention. People want to follow along, simply because it’s different. Or maybe it looks luxurious. Influencers know that, and they know that there is money to be earned from all those eyes on their life. Additionally, Amazon storefronts are quickly getting a footing in the online sphere. There are plenty of creators who make posts reviewing or illustrating a product, and then pointing people to their Amazon storefront to pick up the product themselves. This is marketed as a convenience for the consumer, an easy way to find the exact same product, and it makes the influencer look like a girl’s girl, someone who doesn’t gatekeep good products. Through this practice, influencers make a small profit off of each sale completed through their storefront, kind of like an affiliate link. Promoting a constant wave of new products benefits them and their wallets, but it’s not usually with the consumer's best interest at heart.

 

When consuming and participating in wellness culture, it’s important to remember that there is no magic solution to your health. When a popular product doesn’t make your skin glow, remove your extra fat, and brighten your hair, it’s easy to think that you’re the problem. Unfortunately, when it comes to bodies, it’s usually not as simple as herbal fruit tea, bone broth, greens, or a secret food. Health is determined by a multitude of different factors, including but not limited to, diet, genetics, stress, and environmental factors. Any small thing can throw your health out of wack. It’s impossible to completely control all aspects of your health, even if you have the time and resources to try. So, consume with a grain of salt, and try not to micro-manage your every action when thinking about wellness.
summary: Chasing wellness can give you something new to strive for, a better you. It’s easy to fall into a pattern of seeing impressive people on social media promoting a new tea or a new diet and jumping on the train. It’s a rat race of trying to better yourself through new things, all at the risk of being unhealthy. A wellness culture can be beneficial for making a community and better managing your health, but it can very easily become a toxic obsession. Can wellness culture ever make people feel good about themselves? Let’s take a deeper look.

title: The Host with the Most
content:
Planning your Thanksgiving as a first-time host can be both exciting and overwhelming. Hopefully you’re already well into your Thanksgiving planning, but if not, don’t worry! We’re going to go through everything you need to do so you’re prepared and can sit down, relax, and enjoy Thanksgiving Day. 


Start by writing out your menu, including which guests are bringing what dishes and beverages. Go through all the ingredients you need and do a final fridge and pantry inventory before you leave for the grocery store. Once you have the food, create a timeline. Figure out what foods can be made ahead of time, what needs to cook the longest, and what can be made right before you eat. If you know you’re eating at 7 pm, work backwards from there to figure out when and what you need to start cooking. Vegetables and herbs can be pre-cut and stored in the fridge or freezer until you’re ready to cook. Also, make sure you have enough utensils, crockery, and serving plates, as well as Tupperware and baggies for anyone who wants to take home leftovers. 


Set your table in advance. This gives you time to rearrange and make adjustments without guests at the table. It also gives you a few days to enjoy your centerpieces before you put away your fall decorations. Should great-aunt Mildred be kept away from cousin Casey at all costs? Placecards are a fantastic and subtle way of putting guests where they- and everyone else- will be most comfortable. Having this planned ahead of time also saves you from getting things sorted the day of while food gets cold. 


Accept help! Whether it’s setting the table or helping cook, take help when it’s offered. It gets others involved in the Thanksgiving mood and lifts the burden of doing everything off of your shoulders. After the meal, say yes to anyone who offers to help clean up. Hosting doesn’t mean you can’t sit back and relax with your guests.


At dinner, go around the table and share something you’re grateful for. Especially with a larger group, it’s a great way to learn more about each other and embrace the spirit of giving and thankfulness. And remember: it’s a holiday. Your guests are happy to be spending time with you and not hosting themselves. People are always more forgiving of holiday mishaps than we are of ourselves. 


If you’re a guest this Thanksgiving, you can offer to bring dishes, and help out with set up, clean up, food prep, or with kids. It’s always nice to bring a host or hostess gift in addition to any sides or beverages. Make conversation, engage with others, and have a wonderful Thanksgiving!
summary: Whether you’re a seasoned host or a first- timer, we’ve put together some hosting tips that will keep your Thanksgiving organized and stress- free. Get ready to sit back, relax, and be thankful!

title: Living Your Best Hygge Life
content:
This holiday season, let’s lean in to comfort, coziness, and live our best hygge life. Hygge, pronounced hoo-gah, is a Danish word with no direct translation in English. It loosely translates to a feeling of coziness, inner contentment, and wellbeing. It’s been a key part of Danish culture since at least the 1800’s, when the word first appeared in writing. Hygge is often credited as the reason Denmark regularly places at the top of the World Happiness Report. 


Hygge isn’t just about the things that make you comfortable, but about atmosphere and experiences too. You don’t need to buy all new everything to be hygge. Be purposeful with the things you own, replace and invest in what you need, and intentionally commit your time towards doing things that bring you joy and peace. Anything comfortable, cozy, warm, and simple is hygge. So is being outside and getting fresh air, reading more books, and spending quality time with others. 


Hygge requires all five senses.

Sight: pay attention to the lighting in your space. Fluorescent lights seem to be the default in dorm rooms and many homes. Though they are more energy efficient, the bright glare they give off does nothing for the way we or our spaces look. Shut off the overhead lights and use lamps or fairy lights to create the soft, warm comforting glow hygge is all about. Salt lamps are another great relaxing light source and can purify the air in your home. Candles and firelight are other cozy options. Danes burn more candles than any other country in Europe, about 13 pounds per person per year, thanks largely to hygge. Cozy up to your wood-running or electric fireplace, or stream a burning fire on the tv. 


Smell: Burning candles with scents you enjoy is a great way to relax and set a hygge vibe in your space. You can also make a simmer pot on a stove or hotplate, adding citrus, spices, and essential oils or extracts to boiling water to create a natural and relaxing aroma. Essential oil diffusers are perfect for dorm rooms and other spaces where you can’t have open flames. 


Sound: This depends most on what you find relaxing. Whether you enjoy white noise, music, or silence in your space, embrace whatever makes you feel calm. There are tons of playlists and videos on Spotify and YouTube devoted to hygge vibes you can enjoy. 


Touch: Keep and find things with textures you enjoy, especially those that are soft and comforting. Flannel sheets are a great addition to any bed in cold weather, as are comforters and weighted blankets. Adding throw blankets to chairs and couches will make it easier to sit down and get cozy with a good book and hot drink. You can also incorporate another aspect of hygge, togetherness, by inviting people over to make blankets or other cozy crafts. 


Taste: making comfort food is a large part of embracing hygge. From your favorite soups or slow-cooker meals to baked goods, spend quality time on the food that nourishes you. Food brings people together like nothing else. Have friends over to make charcuterie boards or host a cookie exchange- gathering and connecting is what hygge is all about. 


Elements of hygge can also be brought into home decoration. Focus on natural elements, like wood-based decorations and seasonal greenery. Neutral color schemes with pops of color keeps things simple and comforting without being too cluttered. Speaking of clutter- less is more. Utilize your storage options to give everything in your space a home. Keep it simple!


By prioritizing simplicity, warmth, and connections with others, hygge allows us to enjoy the present while reducing stress. Creating a peaceful atmosphere through soft lighting, comforting surroundings, and meaningful interactions enhances mental health and creates a profound appreciation for life’s small blessings.
summary: Keep things simple, comforting and cozy this season by practicing hygge. Learn more about the practice that’s helped Scandinavian countries place at the top of the World Happiness Index for decades.

title: Immunity Boost: Fact or Fiction?
content:
From bone marrow, where immune cells are made, to the lymph nodes, which release immune cells, to the skin, which protects us from viruses and bacteria, the workings of the immune system are as intricate as it is vital. Despite huge advancements in medicine, there is still much about the immune system that remains unknown.


Full disclaimer: there is no way to ‘boost’ your immune system. Our tissues and organs work as a result of our genetics and lifestyle choices to protect our bodies the best it can. The immune system generally does a fantastic job, but sometimes the immune system alone isn’t enough. 


Vaccines are still the most reliable way to avoid getting sick. Getting a shot isn’t the highlight of anyone’s day, but no one likes getting sick, including the elderly, infants, and immunocompromised individuals who cannot get vaccinated themselves. As we age, our immune systems tend to become less effective. Elderly individuals are more vulnerable to contracting diseases like the flu, COVID-19, and pneumonia, and are more likely to suffer the deadly consequences of these viruses. Sick and immunocompromised individuals tend to rely on herd immunity, which only works when otherwise healthy individuals get vaccinated. Getting your flu shot this fall is the best way to protect yourself, your family and friends, and everyone else you come into close contact with. 


As tempting as it may be, don’t fall for so- called ‘immunity boosting’ supplements. The idea of one gummy a day being enough to keep you healthy is incredibly attractive. These supplements often claim to ‘boost’ your immune system, improving your immune response and strengthening your system. Unfortunately, that’s just not how the immune system works. There are hundreds of different types of cells involved in the immune response, and we just don’t know whether increasing the amounts of certain immune cells or in what ratio to other cells improves immune health. 


Supplements are also not regulated by the FDA, and are therefore not subject to oversight. This allows companies to mislabel their products and mislead consumers. Fortunately, you can purchase supplements that have been approved by third parties, like the United States Pharmacopeia (USP), NSF International, and ConsumerLab, or brands recommended to you by your doctor. 


Other than getting vaccinated and staying away from bogus supplements, there are other ways you can naturally aid your immune system and health. Overall, a healthy lifestyle is key to a healthy immune system. Stress levels are strongly linked to our immune systems and the immune response, though the extent of this relationship is unknown. However, chronic stress is more likely to have a stronger negative impact on an individual's immune health throughout their lifetime. 


Sleep is just important for everything. Just as it gives your brain the opportunity to create memories and retain information, sleep gives the immune system time to work. Sleep loss directly decreases ‘killer’ white blood cell activity, which increases the likelihood of viral infections, cardiovascular and metabolic disorders, and cancer. 


Moderate exercise, like brisk walking, bicycling, swimming, or hiking has been shown to boost the effectiveness of vaccines. Physical activity is also great for cardiovascular health, reducing inflammation and helping immune cells regenerate more often. Exercise also helps reduce stress, so getting as little as 150 minutes of activity a week can help your immune system on two fronts. 


Whether it’s chicken soup or vitamin C, everyone has their go- to cures for when they get sick. Eating well is key to overall immune system health and for recovery after being sick. One link between diet and illness is most commonly seen in the elderly, known as ‘micronutrient malnutrition’. Elderly individuals tend to eat less and stick with familiar foods, which can lead to them not getting enough essential vitamins and minerals provided by diet. The most common deficiencies include zinc, selenium, iron, copper, folic acid, and vitamins A, B6, and E. These have all been shown to alter immune responses in animals and are thought to have a similar role in the human immune system. A simple blood test can reveal whether you’re deficient in any vitamins or minerals, and you can speak with your doctor about dietary changes or taking supplements. 


While there’s no such thing as ‘immune- boosting foods’, there are foods and supplements you can take that relieve symptoms of sickness and help you recover faster. 


Chicken soup: Interestingly, there’s biological evidence that chicken soup can actually help you feel better when you’re sick. It fights inflammation, offers tons of hydration, and loosens mucus while providing a serving of protein and veggies. 


Vitamin C: While vitamin C is effective against colds as a preventative measure, taking it when you’re already sick does nothing. Stick to taking a daily vitamin C supplement as part of your health regiment. Taking vitamin C regularly can lessen the duration and severity of cold and flu symptoms. 


Vitamin D: Vitamin D deficiencies do increase one’s chances of getting sick. However, taking vitamin D if you’re not deficient does nothing for your immune health. Talk to your doctor before taking any supplements. Overdoing it can be just as bad or worse than not getting enough. 


Zinc: Taking zinc lozenges or syrup within 24 hours of developing cold symptoms can shorten the duration of the common cold. Stay away from nasal zinc sprays- they’ve been linked to long- term and permanent loss of smell.


Elderberry: It’s been used in folk medicine for hundreds of years and has become more popular in the mainstream recently. Elderberry contains antioxidants which help prevent developing chronic diseases and can shorten the duration and symptoms of a cold when taken within the first 24 hours. Do not take raw elderberry, as it contains natural compounds that the body converts into cyanide. 


Please speak to your doctor before adding any supplements to your diet. Adding more vitamins or minerals than you need to your diet doesn’t give you additional benefits. Your body just ends up eliminating the excess. It’s also important to know how certain supplements will interact with any current medications or treatments you may be on. For example: you start taking a vitamin D pill once a day without knowing if you’re deficient. Overdosing on vitamin D can cause high calcium levels, which cause nausea/vomiting, constipation, kidney stones, mental and mood changes, and hair loss. Vitamin D supplements can also interfere with medications for cholesterol, weight loss, blood pressure, psoriasis, and your heart, making them less effective and impacting your body’s ability to process vitamin D. 


I can’t promise that following these tips will get you through February without so much as a sniffle, but boosting your overall health and wellness will help with symptoms and illness duration. Embrace a wellness routine and stay hydrated. Tis the season to hibernate, heal, and emerge stronger in the spring.
summary: Is it possible to ‘boost’ your immune system? What healing remedies actually work? Learn about the best way to protect yourself this cold and flu season.

title: Dealing with the Seasonal SADs
content:
We just had our first below 50 degree day where I live in Colorado, and it. was. perfect. Foggy, crisp, orange and yellow leaves being carried everywhere by the wind; it was the quintessential fall day with just a touch of early winter chill. But with this gorgeous seasonal change also comes the realization that the effects of seasonal depression are right around the corner. 


I didn’t experience seasonal depression until my freshman year of college. I went from sunny Colorado (where we get approximately 360 days of sun a year) to Minnesota, where I experienced my first polar vortex and weeks of little to no direct sunlight. Throughout undergrad, I got better at combating seasonal affective disorder, aptly called SAD, and learned lots of management strategies from my classmates and lifelong Midwesterners. 


The specific cause of SAD is still unknown, but the leading theory is that it’s due to a combination of factors. Low sunlight exposure causes disruptions in circadian rhythms and a decrease in naturally occurring serotonin and melatonin. Currently there’s no way to prevent SAD, but early intervention and symptom management is key to reducing symptoms and staying balanced. 


Beginning in the fall, plan weekly activities with friends, family, or by yourself. Engaging in these activities frequently will help elevate your mood heading into the winter months and get you into a pattern. It’s a lot harder to try to create a schedule and keep plans when you’re depressed and tired, so maintaining plans in advance ensures that creating fun time for yourself becomes a habit.


Maintaining a regular sleep and wake schedule is key. People with SAD often report trouble falling asleep and staying awake, likely because low sunlight levels throw off natural circadian rhythms and melatonin levels. Keeping a regular bedtime and morning routine can alleviate these symptoms. It also exposes your body to light at predictable times, which will help re-establish natural body rhythms. Taking melatonin supplements can also help if you’re having trouble sleeping. 


One of the most common treatments for SAD is bright light therapy. You can purchase bright light boxes on Amazon, and many doctors and therapists offer bright light treatment in the winter as well. These boxes give off light that mimics sunlight, which helps reset your circadian rhythm and boosts mood. A friend of mine in college swore by her light box and would bring it to our weekly study sessions during the winter, and I always left feeling more energized, rested, and optimistic than when I started. 


Vitamin D has also been linked to SAD. Vitamin D can be taken in through one’s diet, but our bodies also make vitamin D naturally in response to sunlight. People living further from the equator (who typically experience less sunlight during the year) are more likely to have vitamin D deficiencies and suffer from depression/ SAD. Taking vitamin D supplements can have neuroprotective qualities and alleviate SAD symptoms. Adding more vitamin D rich foods to your diet, like eggs, fish, and mushrooms, can also help. 


If you’re able to, get out of town! Head somewhere sunnier and warmer for a bit and enjoy a much- needed change in scenery. Can’t get out for a vacay? Plan a staycation. Get out and explore new activities, restaurants, and experiences near you. Whether you’re in Minneapolis or Miami, enjoying yourself outdoors will keep you regulated and energized.


Exercise helps with all forms of depression, and SAD is no exception. It also helps combat weight gain, which many people with and without SAD experience in the winter months. Outdoor exercise is the most helpful for SAD symptoms as it combines exercise and increased sunlight exposure. Even if it’s not direct sunlight, you’ll still reap the benefits of increased vitamin D and serotonin levels. Let light indoors, and work near natural sources of light if you can. 


Winter is such a wonderful time of the year, and with these tips you can get the most out of your holiday season. Being proactive now will pay off later by ensuring you get the most of the season’s delights. Enjoy sweater weather, seasonal treats, and connecting with loved ones knowing you can handle anything this winter throws at you.

title: Interview with Endrina Sánchez
content:
This week we spoke with Endrina Sánchez, a Costa Rican-born artist who designed the amazing new GrasshoppHer podcast cover. A designer, digital illustrator, and muralist, she’s a triple threat with a focus on nature and the beautiful landscapes around her. 


Endri had a passion for art early on. “I have good memories from my childhood of my relationship with art, although I grew up in a town that lacked good education, I always had a passion for creating. I participated in competitions and stood out from others.”


Endri graduated from the University of Costa Rica in Graphic Design with an emphasis on plastic arts. Digital illustration allows Endri to “play with elements, beautify spaces and be myself. I love being able to create my own illustrations that others might like. It is a way to share with others, [and] a special feeling.” After her professional training, she traveled with other artists throughout the country in a studio on wheels creating visual content. “This experience was very enriching and inspiring due to the wonderful landscapes and particular situations [I experienced].”


It was on this journey that she discovered surfing. “I fell deeply in love with the environment that surrounds this sport. Since then I have largely dedicated myself to digital illustration inspired by the lifestyle that accompanies surfing, nature, and landscape, among other things.” 


Endri currently lives in Nosara, Costa Rica, an area known for its amazing beaches and active surfing community. After the Spanish destroyed most of the natural landscape in Nosara to support cattle. Beginning in the 60’s, the forest began to rebound and the Ostional National Wildlife Reserve was established in 1983 to protect the beaches, shoreline, and natural habitats of local wildlife. Additionally, Nosara is considered a Blue Zone, an area where people commonly and comfortably live to be over 100 years old due to good air and water quality, great food, and many opportunities for active lifestyles. 


Maintaining balance has been a lifelong pursuit which has required Endri to make many decisions, and sometimes sacrifices. “I chose to live and work in a natural environment that transmits peace and freedom to me, although for this I have had to sacrifice other things such as greater stability, comfort, or closeness with my family.” Through seeking balance, Endri has learned to “take my space, not to force my tasks, sometimes getting away from my daily work processes… breathing and coming back [to something] helps me a lot.” 


Endri also maintains a healthy work- life balance by spending time with friends or her two pets; an orange cat, Suppli, and an Australian cattle dog, Nube. 


Visit Endri’s website or Instagram @vroomtraits to see her beautiful work and available products.
summary: We interviewed artist Endrina Sánchez to learn more about her art, her journey, and the pursuit of balance

title: Using Creativity to Heal
content:
Using Creativity to Heal

My nephew often wants to play with me after family dinner. Being at the table makes him antsy, sitting still is definitely not his style. He always bolts up, grabs my hand, and drags me out to the backyard with him. He’ll take me to his secret hiding spots, a place near the shed and the faded wooden fence, or behind the tree with an old bird’s nest in it. He’ll explain the updated politics of the local wildlife and fictional woodland creatures (there is an ongoing conflict between the moss fairies and the pigeons). He often times has me prepare for an epic sword battle between us and the twigs or leaves around the yard. He’ll patch my battle wounds with liquid bandages (mud) and give an inspiring speech about our victory. We always get to celebrate because it’s the world that he created. He is in control of the narrative, which empowers him to adventure into new territories and conquer his fears.

 

This kind of creativity is most present in children. You don’t have to direct them to create, they often dance, sing, and play all on their own. They want to create and are prompted to by their explorations of the world. Each piece of knowledge means that there is a wealth of questions to explore. They want to fill in the gaps with something fantastical. Producing creative ideas often decreases with age. Kids discover the real answers to their questions which are most often more plain than what they imagined. As they age, they are given increasingly less space to explore their creativity. School environments encourage good behavior and force structure, which often involves sitting at a desk and doing their work quietly. School quickly becomes a place of boredom and imposed ideas, which doesn’t foster creativity very well. This kind of environment for an extended period of time stunts creative growth. School eventually turns into the workplace, which often follows the same ideas of quiet structure. It's not very often that we’re asked to come up with our own ideas. We consume media that makes ideas for us, tells us how to live our daily lives and how to navigate relationships. In the workplace, corporate ideals are often pushing for new ideas and innovation to gain a new consumer base. Even so, these innovations must be in a way that is approved by the company. It's more, "here’s a new idea, learn it" than "can you help us come up with new ideas". We are taught by our environments early on to follow, not to lead.

 

Employers are now playing with the idea of fostering more creativity within the workspace. We can see shifts in the ideas surrounding the work environment. Cubicles are becoming open-plan offices, more lounges are being implemented, and there is an encouragement to play during work, but just enough to make you better at your job. It sounds counterintuitive, but research has shown that being bored can actually help foster creativity. Repetitive tasks and boredom help people embrace daydreaming, which makes space for creativity. Lots of people zone out during boring tasks, which may actually be a good thing for a creative nature. Getting to create within the workplace can be personally motivating and exciting, as well as increase productivity. You’re more likely to do your work if you’re engaged with it, and you’re more likely to be engaged if you created it!

Not only is creativity valuable in the workplace, but it can also help in your personal life. People often use creative outlets to work through personal hardship or even traumatic experiences. You may have heard about this through music or art therapy, and the breakthrough discoveries surrounding the use of art in mental health. Artistic expression is a powerful medium, and it can harbor many experiences, good or bad. Creating something can act as a catalyst to hold space for a negative experience in a healthy way. People often describe that creativity makes approaching and coping with hardship easier. It makes an accessible pathway to experience.

 

Creating can also act as a way to connect to a deeper part of yourself. Writers often talk about how the work writes through them, exposing a part of themselves that they may have forgotten or been hesitant to visit. It can also act as a way to connect to others. There is always some level of relatability in human experience, and sharing your creative works with others may help them to better understand you as well as relate to you. It can also give a sense of empowerment, accomplishment, and pride. There’s something about making an original product that is extremely powerful. It’s easy to take pride in making something beautiful, or even just something new.

 

Creativity is a powerful tool in its own right. It can help with motivation and productivity at work as well as healing and self-exploration on a personal level. Creating is great medicine, and it can provide a deep safe space for introspection. No one wants to stay hurt forever, and creativity can act as a way to work through personal and professional hardships. It’s a multi-purpose skill that anyone can learn and refine. What will you do with your creativity?

title: The Key to Effortless Small Talk
content:
There’s a widely held perception that people hate small talk. Small talk is made out to be boring and awkward, but in reality? It’s the foundation of nearly all meaningful personal and professional relationships and an incredibly vital skill to have. 


So many things start with a small conversation. Interviews, dates, networking events, social gatherings- it’s good to know how to talk to people and it’s important that you feel confident in your ability to do so. In some situations, small talk can be more important than the main conversation. In an interview, for example, small talk can provide a better sense of who you are as a candidate than typical interview questions that one can prepare for ahead of time. There’s more at stake when there’s no ‘right’ answer, and your responses and ability to converse say a lot about you and your personality that more formal questions might not reveal. 


When people think of small talk, they usually imagine the dreaded “how’s the weather” conversation that lasts forever. Easy topics like the weather are the foundations of small talk, but you have to build upon that foundation. For example, say you start a conversation with someone about the weather. Once you’ve both made a comment, see if you can pivot the conversation to a related but more interesting topic. Do you have weekend plans that depend on good weather? Maybe you’re going camping, and the person you’re talking to goes every year. Are your yard and flowers benefitting from the rain? Maybe the other person has their own herb garden, or knows someone who grows their own produce. By simply branching out to a more personal topic, you’ve shifted a simple conversation about the weather to a discussion that helps you get to know someone better.


I went to a Body Shop outlet about two years ago, after lockdown ended but before the mask mandate had been lifted. The store was completely empty aside from the employee and myself, so I made conversation to fill that dreaded awkward silence. The employee said hi, I reciprocated, and we had a nice conversation about it being nice to be out in public again. It turns out we had both gotten dogs right before the pandemic hit, and we bonded over our pups and meeting other dog owners on our daily pandemic walks. When I was about to check out, the employee told me to go pick out a few things for free. The reason? Because they could tell I smiled at them, even under the mask, and the conversation we had had was the longest and nicest customer interaction they’d had in a while. 


One of the main reasons people dislike small talk is because they lack confidence in social interactions, or are afraid of feeling embarrassed by saying the wrong thing. Believe me, I understand. Somewhere between seventh and eighth grade I developed severe social anxiety, to the point where I wouldn’t answer questions in class because I was afraid of answering wrong and having people think I wasn’t smart, or even that people would think my voice was weird. I was able to build up my confidence and grew more comfortable speaking aloud just in time for the end of high school and college, when I had to speak publicly and give presentations frequently.


Fortunately (or perhaps unfortunately), the solution to this social anxiety is simple- put yourself in more social situations. Pay attention to how different people communicate, especially those you think of as confident conversationalists. Watch and listen to what they say, what they don’t say, and what communication strategies work best with different people. Then put yourself in their position! One easy way to do this is by showing up to a meeting or class a little early and making conversation with whoever is there. You can also stay a little late and make conversation on your way out. 


It can help to change how you think about small talk and conversations in general. Alison Wood Brooks, an associate professor of Business Administration at Harvard Business School, recommends framing these conversations as a treasure hunt. The ‘treasure’ is new information or details about a person, and the questions you ask are your tools. Reframing conversations as an exciting game that you have chosen to engage in helps your brain reframe the action of being social into a positive and enjoyable experience instead of something that causes you stress. 


Being in a new social environment often makes us feel like we’re surrounded by strangers, awkwardly waiting for someone else to break the ice. In reality, every situation offers “free information”, a term coined by Corporate Motivational Speaker Debra Fine, that you can use to start a good conversation. Say you’re at a baby shower for a friend, but you don’t know anyone else there. One thing you do know is that everyone there also knows your friend. You can use the question about how someone knows the mom-to-be as a launching point for a conversation, paying attention to details in the conversation that let you take it to the next level. 


It’s impossible to have a productive conversation without active listening. If you’re more focused on what you’re saying than listening to the other person, you need to switch your focus. Paying attention to the other person will help you ask relevant questions and engage in the conversation. You can throw in nonverbal cues that let the other person know subconsciously that you’re engaged and focused on them. In general, making eye contact, nodding, and having open gestures and posture are all signs of good listening and engagement. It helps to actually be interested in what the other person is saying, but I’d be lying if I said that was always possible in every conversation you have. Regardless of the quality of conversation, practicing active listening will ensure that your conversation partners always feel seen and think of you as a good listener and conversationalist.  


Ask open ended questions! A conversation dies when you ask questions that can be answered with “yes” or “no”. Asking more complex questions not only shows that you’re interested in what someone has to say, but helps get them engaged. Questions you ask in one conversation become follow-up points for later. If you know someone just became a parent, check in with them about how their kid is doing, or see how a coworker is liking their new promotion. Remembering important details makes people feel seen, listened to, and contributes to building strong relationships. 


The best conversations are a two- way street, and the exchange of information needs to flow both ways. Sharing personal anecdotes with someone creates common ground and builds rapport over shared experiences. In a conversation, make sure there’s a good sense of give and take between who’s sharing and responding. A good conversation shouldn’t feel like an interrogation either. If you’re talking with someone about their new dog, for example, interject questions with conversation. You could ask about what breed the dog is, if they’ve had dogs before, or how they’re enjoying having a puppy. In between these questions, share some of your own experiences; like a dog you had when you were younger of the same breed or your experiences dogsitting a puppy. You should both leave the interaction with a sense of the other person’s experience and personality. 


Compliments can also be a great way to start some small talk. If you’re going to compliment someone, there are a few do’s and don'ts. Generally speaking, avoid complimenting someone’s features or appearance. These types of compliments can easily cross the line into being inappropriate, especially if the person being complimented is of a different gender or holds a lower position than you. However, a compliment about a close friend and coworker’s makeup is different from the same compliment given to a relative stranger-  use your best discretion. Focus on a form of personal expression, like jewelry, accessories, or even tattoos instead. Whether you’re complimenting someone’s bracelet or their choice in pen, expressing an interest in things will usually lead to details about the individual. Not only will you know more about the person after your conversation, but they will feel closer to you and small talk with them will be more comfortable in the future. 


By actively listening, asking open- ended questions, and genuinely interacting with others, you can improve your small talk skills. Practice is key, so don’t be afraid to be the one to initiate conversation and take risks. You’ll be confidently conversing with strangers in no time!
summary: While it might seem like some people are just born gifted conversationalists, getting better at small talk is something anyone can do with the right tools. It only takes a few days to feel more confident in your conversation skills!

title: Long Covid Fatigue in the Workplace
content:
The effects of the pandemic are still lingering. There are artifacts of it everywhere, disposed masks on the streets, empty hand sanitizer dispensers, and stickers prompting people to stand six feet apart. One of the places where the ghost of Covid is most prevalent is the workplace. We have seen that long Covid and new outbreaks or strains repeatedly prevent people from returning to work. Additionally, many in the workforce are experiencing Covid fatigue, a long-lasting feeling of exhaustion that has been compared to chronic fatigue syndrome. This exhaustion can be caused by Covid-19, but it’s also relevant to people just trying to get by in a post-lockdown world.

 

With the declaration of the pandemic came increased levels of stress and uncertainty. Many individuals lost their jobs and were forced to stay at home, which led to financial stress and feelings of social isolation. It was a difficult time, to say the least. People were afraid of becoming sick which led to skepticism and distrust among communities, fracturing previously strong bonds. These kinds of negative feelings don’t just fade away. For many, lingering reminders about the not-so-distant past induce stress and anxiety. Most still experience lasting financial instability and fears for the future.

 

In addition to the emotional turmoil, there is more evidence surfacing about the effects of Covid and the diagnosis of long Covid. It has been reported that some people who have been infected with Covid are experiencing symptoms for three months or more. This then becomes diagnosed as long Covid, with symptoms persisting for at least two months with no other explanation. These symptoms include fatigue, anxiety, depression, and memory difficulties. Due to a loss of support for people suffering from Covid and the haste to return to life as normal, many are forced to return to work despite having these negative symptoms. Studies have shown that this diagnosis disproportionately affects women, along with the elderly and those who are lower income.

 

It seems overwhelming at times, and yet we keep moving forward. We have faced all of these negatives and somehow made it through, so how can we keep pushing when experiencing Covid-induced fatigue? There are some strategies that we can employ to help mitigate this lingering fatigue. One approach is to establish a stable routine. Much of the anxiety that came with Covid is based on the rapid change that we experienced and the uncertainty about what the future will hold. Making a set routine is a simple way to combat this feeling of insecurity in everyday life. It provides stability and day-to-day activities, as well as gives each day a purpose. It can also prove to be grounding in the whirlwind of change. Even if you find consistency in the small things like your cup of coffee in the morning, that simple gesture can provide some soothing and put you a little more at ease.

 

Another way to combat this fatigue is to utilize your social network. The people in your community often feel similarly about situations, and that kind of support group gives you a safe space to discuss your feelings. It can definitely help to air your frustrations, fears, and feelings in general. It may feel like these conversations are pointless like you’re just complaining but not finding a way to solve the problem. These kinds of conversations provide something incredibly important: human connection. We all want to feel heard and seen, and talking about these issues can help us connect with our peers. Talking about things also helps us to rationalize, experience, and cope with difficult times or feelings.

 

One of the most important strategies to combating Covid-induced fatigue is to give yourself grace. All of us are still recovering from this incredibly stressful and still ongoing experience. It has affected all of us, both personally and professionally. It affects the way that we do, experience, and think about things. The ghost of Covid is still lingering everywhere, in all of us, there is no shame in being affected by this hardship. It’s okay to have off days or to be less productive than usual because this is an unusual time. It’s important to make space for yourself in this process and to care for yourself in the way that best helps you.

 

Long Covid fatigue is incredibly prevalent today. We can see it everywhere and in every person. Everything is affected by the ghost of Covid, and it doesn’t look like that feeling will be fading anytime soon. Even so, we continue to persevere and try to make a new sense of normalcy in a world that is post-lockdown.

title: Get the Best Sleep of Your Life
content:
I firmly believe that a good nap can cure anything. Bad mood? Take a nap. Feeling sick? Take a nap. Getting worn down? Take a nap. As fundamental as sleep is, we do an astonishing number of things during the day that negatively impact our nights.


I wasn’t a believer in the power of sleep until high school. Taking a fifteen minute nap after class or making sure I got more than six hours of sleep a night went a long way in improving my day and making me more productive. 


When I started senior year of college, I hit a wall. I was trying to get to bed by 11, but as hard as I tried I just couldn’t fall asleep. I’d listen to music, sleep meditations, and toss and turn until I finally passed out, usually around 4-5 am the next morning. During the day, I was drinking coffee like it was my job and falling asleep in my early morning lectures. By the time class and work was over, I’d go home exhausted, take a nap, and then settle back in for homework and extracurriculars. By nighttime, I’d be physically exhausted but mentally wide awake.


Looking back, it took longer than I’d like to admit to get help. As a college student, no one I knew was getting enough sleep, and plenty of people got by with caffeine and naps. Sleep seems to be the first thing we write off when faced with more important duties. As a student, new parent, or a professional, sleep has become an expected and sometimes necessary sacrifice. However, this sleep loss isn’t sustainable. Just because we can run on four hours of sleep a night doesn’t mean we should. 


After consulting with my doctor, I was diagnosed with insomnia and prescribed a sleep medication. The change was radical. I could go to sleep by eleven and wake up in the morning without any tiredness. However, we also talked about the importance of creating a restful nighttime routine. While the medication made it so that I could sleep, getting restful sleep and creating a calming environment was on me. After doing lots and lots of research, these were the most valuable practices that revolutionized my sleep. 


There’s only so much you can do with a standard dorm twin XL mattress. While pricey, investing in a good mattress pad and mattress topper can make a huge difference in your quality of sleep. If you’ve got an otherwise uncomfortable mattress, it’s probably time to upgrade! Luckily, the month of September is a great time to do it. September 30th marks the end of the fiscal year for many businesses, and mattress retailers are likely to mark down prices in order to sell as much product as possible before the end of the month. Online mattress retailers are less likely to offer discounts, as their products are often cheaper to begin with, but they do tend to offer discounted mattress and bedding bundles. It’s recommended to replace your mattress after seven years- see if you’re overdue for a boost. I upgraded my mattress topper and mattress pad for versions that offered more support and cushion, and I’ve never looked back! I noticed a big difference in the amount of stiffness I felt after sleeping and was much more comfortable overall when falling asleep.


The amount of light present when you sleep is another huge factor in sleep quality. Your eyes perceive light even when you’re asleep, and they send messages to your brain that it’s time to wake up. In the past, circadian rhythms were naturally more attuned to sunrise and sunset, but the advent of electric lights and modern electronics have interfered with these natural rhythms. It’s best to sleep in as much darkness as possible. Shutting your eyes often isn’t enough. The windows in my dorm had standard metal blinds, but the streetlamps outside and passing headlights cast light that made its way into my room regardless. So, I got a cheap expandable curtain rod that didn’t require screws and found short blackout curtains at Target. Sleeping in pitch black was much more relaxing and provided less for my brain to focus on when I was trying to sleep. If you can sleep with an eye mask, do it! It’s an easy fix for getting rid of ambient light, especially if you’re on a different sleep routine than a roommate or partner.


I was also unknowingly around too much light when getting ready for bed. I would go straight from doing homework and eating dinner with my lights on to trying to sleep. Dimming lights closer to bedtime or changing light colors to red, orange, and yellow creates a more relaxing ambiance that provides less light. You’ve heard it before, but I’ll say it again- screen time before bed is a huge factor in not getting restful sleep. Reducing the amount of blue light typically produced by electronics is vital. I was very, very guilty of using my phone up to bedtime, and even though I was listening to calming music or sleep meditations the blue light was really affecting my circadian rhythm.


An hour before bed, even if I wasn’t done with homework, I would turn my room lights off and use my fairy lights or a lamp instead. I also started listening to music and meditations and set my alarms around this same time and turning my phone off so I didn’t have an excuse to use it before bed.


The last change I made was creating a relaxing pre-sleep ritual. Like I mentioned, I would end most nights going straight from doing homework to my bath routine and then to bed within ten minutes. Even though I felt exhausted, this wasn’t enough of a break for my brain to shut off and for me to get relaxed before bed. I started by forcing myself to do something relaxing for ten minutes before going to sleep. I would read, crochet, take time for my skincare routine, and do yoga. Having a screen free outlet for my stress and energy at the end of the day helped me relax before sleeping and led to me feeling more naturally tired. 


It may seem obvious, but make sure you’re comfortable. Are you a warm or a cold sleeper? Do you like to be swaddled in blankets, or are you content with a light sheet? If you have neck or back pain, learn which sleeping positions offer more support and relief. Going to bed knowing what relaxes you will reduce tossing, turning and the chance of waking up uncomfortable.


If you prioritize a consistent sleep schedule and create a comfortable sleep environment, you’ll wake up refreshed and ready to take on anything. Good nights lead to great days!
summary: Getting good sleep is essential for our physical and mental well-being. The quality of the sleep we get is much more important than the quantity. Learn more about best sleep practices and revitalize your rest!

title: Community: How it Can Help You Overcome Setbacks
content:
When you’re having a hard time, have you had people tell you to call someone you love? It sounds cheesy, right? How can calling one person solve all of your problems? The quick answer is they won’t, but they can provide crucial support and a sense of belonging. That feeling of connection to another person makes interacting with your community invaluable. When experiencing setbacks in your career or personal life, relying on the community around you can help you persevere and overcome.

 

How do you define community? At the baseline, a community is a group of people connected by one or more commonalities. This common tie could be anything, think family, peers, friends, neighbors, or even coworkers. It is almost impossible to not be involved in some sort of community. These groups of people can be extremely steady like family, or they can be ever-changing, like coworkers or neighbors. This kind of fluidity can provide a rich collection of perspectives and resources. This also means that there is almost always someone or a group of people around to help you with a variety of issues.

 

Communities provide social connection and a sense of belonging that is crucial to personal well-being. A lack of these two important factors can be detrimental to mental and physical health, as most of us personally experienced during the recent pandemic. In times like what we went through during lockdown, where there is a deep feeling of personal isolation, it can lead to a steep decrease in mental health. This kind of deep decline can lead to an increase in health risk factors and damage physical health. Additionally, feelings of loneliness have been linked to increased levels of stress, increased risk of depression, and increased sleep impairment, all of which can harm mental and physical wellness. Community interaction can help to prevent these negative symptoms and aid personal healing.

 

Another important benefit of being involved in a community is the safe space that it can provide. There is something deeply powerful about a group of people united by a common thread or passion. This kind of connection can be energizing and reassuring simultaneously. It can bring a sort of comforting normalcy, sometimes it can help to just have a conversation about something different than what’s bothering you. This kind of social satisfaction can also act as a mental resetting point, which can give you more motivation to tackle the setback that you’ve been experiencing. A community can easily become an essential safe space to regularly incorporate into your routine.

 

When experiencing a setback professionally, the community can be one of your most important resources. A group of people can give many material resources, but the people themselves can act as a gift. Oftentimes, meeting and speaking with other people can provide inspiration. Diverse perspectives and new ideas can prompt you to work against your setbacks, or at least provide you with a good place to start. Even just talking to someone and seeing a different point of view can spark new ideas and solutions. This kind of inspiration is hard to come by when searching other places, and the community is a great place to start looking.

 

When experiencing a hardship personally, a community can provide an intimate form of support. People often reach out to the people closest to them when they are going through something in their personal life. This group of people can provide reassurance just in the fact that they support you. People are around you for a reason and having that kind of safety net to fall back on can be incredibly reassuring. They can also provide support in the form of verbal reassurance. This is a more direct motivator but is usually effective in providing reassurance and encouragement. Knowing that others believe in you, especially those whom you value the opinions of, can be extremely motivating. Even without brilliant advice or shiny new ideas, sometimes simple encouragement is enough to help you persevere.

 

Everyone needs support from their community, and there is no shame in seeking out help when experiencing personal or professional hardship. The community provides both practical resources and deep emotional support. It makes a safe space for friendship and resilience to grow. Most people will be willing to assist you in some way, and almost all will be more than willing to simply have a conversation with you. All it takes is some reaching out.
summary: When you’re having a hard time, have you had people tell you to call someone you love? It sounds cheesy, right? How can calling one person solve all of your problems? The quick answer is they won’t, but they can provide crucial support and a sense of belonging. That feeling of connection to another person makes interacting with your community invaluable. When experiencing setbacks in your career or personal life, relying on the community around you can help you persevere and overcome.

title: Embrace the Flavors of Fall
content:
Starbucks has released everything pumpkin spice, and you know what means- it’s officially fall! Though warm weather is sticking around, spooky season, changing leaves and Thanksgiving are all right around the corner. Lean in to the season and explore new recipes that showcase fall produce, while helping your local farmers and reducing your carbon footprint by eating in-season goods. The comfy, cozy vibes of fall are perfect for getting the family involved in baking and cooking


Whether you’re cooking for one or starting to train your mini sous-chef, fall is the perfect time to experiment with new recipes. The comfy, cozy vibes of the season are perfect for staying in and spending time in the kitchen. 


While it’s extremely convenient to be able to find things like peaches and tomatoes year- round, there are some great benefits to eating in-season produce. In-season produce is fresher, and as a result tastes better and has more nutrients. Storing produce for longer periods of time leads to a decrease in nutrients like Vitamin C and folate, and produce can even be irradiated and preserved in wax to extend shelf life. 


Produce is also typically cheaper when purchased in- season, since it’s locally sourced and requires less to transport and store on the way to the grocery store. It’s also more environmentally friendly and reduces your carbon footprint.


The timing of produce seasonality is fascinating. Citrus fruits are typically in season from winter to spring, which seems odd given the warm, humid climates they grow best in. However, the vitamin C provided by citrus fruits are a key nutrient in helping prevent colds and the flu. In- season winter vegetables all contain vitamins that help boost your immune system and reduce inflammation, which helps prevent against getting sick and reduces symptoms like pain, fatigue, and insomnia. Summer produce, like peaches and other stone fruits, are full of carotenoids which help protect your skin from sun damage and sunburn. 


Pumpkins are a staple of the season, but there’s so much more to do with them besides jack-o-lanterns and making pumpkin seeds. From sweet pumpkin bread or pumpkin spice latte bundt cake to savory pumpkin ravioli with brown butter and sage, its versatility ensures that every meal is a hit. (Fun fact: pumpkins are somehow considered a squash, a gourd, and a fruit). 


We’ll say it- sweet potatoes are better than regular potatoes. Try easy oven- baked sweet potato fries or a savory fall Buddha bowl with sweet potatoes, chickpeas, and kale. This candied sweet potato recipe is the most demanded Thanksgiving side in my family for a reason- try it this fall for an instant hit! 


Fall is peak pear season. Unlike most fruits, pears start to ripen once they’re at room temperature after being picked, so they’ve got a longer shelf life than most other produce. Try an easy pear, arugula and brie panini for lunch, or add to oatmeal for a delicious and nutritious breakfast. For a classic dessert, try this spiced pear crisp with a scoop of vanilla ice cream. 


Enjoy!
summary: Experiment with these and other recipes, get creative in the kitchen, and discover new favorites!

title: Free Fall Fun
content:
Having a good time doesn’t have to mean spending money this fall. There are plenty of fun and cost- effective activities to help you embrace the beauty and spirit of the season. As the leaves change and the air gets crisper, embrace the simple things and spare your wallet. 


Start a daily journal. Something about fall just makes it the perfect time to start journaling. Maybe it’s the changing scenery, or the cooler weather, or the upcoming holidays, but there’s a lot to think and reflect on this time of year. Great news- making time for your mental and emotional well-being is always free. Putting your thoughts to paper is a great practice that can help your productivity, stress, and emotional stability this fall. 


Go to your local library. When was the last time you checked out some books? Visit your local library and look around. Many libraries offer family- friendly story time and children’s activities if you’re bringing littles along. Catch up on your TBR list or discover a new audiobook or movie. Just don’t forget to return your books before their due date or you could be paying a late fine. 


Shift your wardrobe over to fall. Those summer shorts and tank tops are cute, but maybe not as practical for the upcoming months. Going through your closet and taking out your summer fits will give you much more closet space (which we could all use a little more of) for those bulkier fall and winter items. Not only will this help you see what you already have and what you need, but you can sort through all your clothes and sell or donate items to a local consignment or thrift store. A cleaner closet goes a long way to reducing stress over outfit planning in the mornings.


Host a game night with friends. Invite friends over for a night in and play some games! Everyone can bring a game to play or appetizers and drinks so you don't get saddled with sole cooking responsibilities. For something new, host a PowerPoint night. Everyone picks a different topic involving guests, like “Most Likely to Survive a Bear Attack” or “Who Would Win the Hunger Games” and presents their slideshow. All you really need for a great time are food, drinks, and some hot takes. Fall is the perfect time to make some memories and spend quality time with loved ones.


Visit a local park, wildlife reserve, or national park. Pack a picnic lunch and a book and head outside! Parks and reserves often offer educational programs about wildlife and conservation for all ages. Escape the hustle and bustle and take in the weather and changing colors while getting a healthy dose of fresh air. You can also enjoy fall activities usually held in open areas, like pumpkin picking and corn mazes. If you’re lucky enough to live by a national park, check it out! Just know that most parks charge a small entry fee that goes towards park maintenance. 


Stay in bed and binge watch a new series. There’s nothing better than waking up in the morning and not having anything to do. Take advantage of a weekend or a day off to stay in your pjs, wrap up in a cozy blanket, and park yourself in front of a screen to binge a new series. There’s always new content coming to streaming services, and whether you're into reality tv or the season finale of a fan favorite show, there’s plenty of options to choose from.  


Go on a nature walk. You may be sensing a theme here. Fall really is the perfect time to get outside- temperatures are cooler, scenery is gorgeous, and you don’t have to worry about being swarmed by bugs. If you’re anything like me, nothing productive happens outside unless it’s below 70 degrees. Nature walks have been shown to improve exercise habits, reduce stress, enhance vitamin D production and boost your immune system. For an added bonus, you can listen to music or a podcast while you’re out.
summary: Check out our budget friendly ideas for enjoying the fall season! Whether you’re by yourself or with others, you’ll be able to balance having fun and saving money.

title: How To Choose A Bank That Fits You
content:
Choosing a financial institution to handle your money is an incredibly important financial decision. Where you store your money acts as a basis for all of your financials, as you are reliant on this institution to care for your money according to your needs. National banks, regional banks, credit unions, and online banks all offer differing services, rates, and fees. These differences may be confusing or simply overwhelming, and your financial needs shift throughout life. It’s always beneficial to shop the market of financial institutions, so how do you find a bank that fits you?


The first step to choosing a financial institution that best fits your needs is to establish what kind of account you’re looking for. The basic account types are checking and savings, but there are also certificates of deposit accounts (CDs) and money market accounts. Each account type has a specific purpose and role within personal finance, with most of the difference being about spending or saving.


·      Checking accounts: These accounts are used for everyday spending needs. They typically have a debit card associated with the account and ATM access for ease of accessing the money within the account. This is typically used for withdrawals rather than deposits, meaning more money typically goes out rather than in. It’s better to keep a lower balance in these accounts since there is no interest accrued on the money within the account.


·      Savings accounts: These accounts are used for short-term saving and garnering interest. This is where you would put leftover money at the end of the month for a rainy day later on. Typically, these accounts have an interest rate, which adds a small amount of money to your account each month based on your balance in the account. You can basically get a very small amount of free money each month. The more you deposit, the bigger your interest return will be. There is typically no card associated with these accounts, and access to the money within the account differs between institutions. Consider money less accessible than a checking account.


·      Certificates of deposit: A certificate of deposit is a sum of money that is locked in an account for a specific amount of time with fixed interest. CDs are good for larger savings/purposes, but you want to make sure that you will not need to access this money, as if you break the time there is often a fee associated. The common lock time for CDs is five years. They act as a good way to make a lasting relationship with a financial institution and allow you to save a sum of money with a specific purpose rather than general savings. People often use CDs for larger purposes like businesses, houses, cars, etc.


·      Money market account: These accounts act like savings accounts but with more withdrawal options. It’s kind of like the midpoint between checking and savings, with a debit card and ATM service and interest. They may limit the transactions within the account, but these limits are typically higher than that of a savings account. Think of it as a savings account with greater accessibility.


Deciding what kind of account you want to open allows you to better evaluate which financial institution to entrust your money to.


There are a multitude of different financial institutions for you to choose from currently. There are physical banks along with fully online banks, and each choice has pros and cons. It’s important to assess what features are important to you and which aren’t.


National banks are brick-and-mortar institutions, meaning that they have a physical location for you to visit. Their services are largely in-person, with some online banking capability and access to ATM services. There are usually monthly fees associated with accounts at national banks, along with low savings interest rates, and overdraft fees, but they are generally easily accessible. There are usually many locations nationwide, making these banks prominent in the financial industry.


Regional banks (also known as community or local banks) are also brick-and-mortar institutions that are typically focused on a region or community. These banks are usually known for their “relationship-based” banking, where the institution has a relationship with its customers. These banks are also known for being friendly towards small/local businesses in the area, providing loans and other services to the locals. Most of these banks are also community development financial institutions (CDFIs), which provide funds to low-income communities. These banks may lack the newest technology, but they provide ATM access and some mobile banking capability.


Credit unions are not-for-profit banks. These institutions are often community-focused or regional, with membership requirements to join the institution. These requirements could be living in a certain area, a business association, or just general demographics. Credit unions typically have high savings interest rates, resulting in a better return on your money. These institutions are run by the members rather than having profit-focused motivations. They also may lack the latest technology for mobile banking, as they mainly provide in-person services.


Online banks are exactly as they sound, a bank that provides full online services. They usually have high savings interest rates, since they are typically cheaper to maintain than a brick-and-mortar institution. There are low fees associated with accounts at online banks, but there are also some cons associated with banking completely online. These banks are often not “full-service”, meaning that they may only offer one type of account per bank, and they have no ATM access. There is also very little customer service, and the customer service that is available is often sub-par. Even so, these banks are incredibly convenient and accessible for a multitude of people.


At the end of the day, choosing a bank is an important financial decision that heavily relies on what your financial goals are. Each institution has different strengths and weaknesses, and it’s common for your financial needs to change throughout life. Shopping in the bank market can help you get a better deal for your money and better support for your financial journey.
summary: Choosing a financial institution to handle your money is an incredibly important financial decision. Where you store your money acts as a basis for all of your financials, as you are reliant on this institution to care for your money according to your needs. National banks, regional banks, credit unions, and online banks all offer differing services, rates, and fees. These differences may be confusing or simply overwhelming, and your financial needs shift throughout life. It’s always beneficial to shop the market of financial institutions, so how do you find a bank that fits you?
