title: Unlocking Happiness: The Power of Gratitude
content:
I’ve been keeping a gratitude journal on and off since I was young. It was a practice my mom encouraged me to start in elementary school, jotting down three to five things I was grateful for in one of the many pretty journals I had accumulated. Looking back at my old journals, I’m amazed by how little has changed between now and then. I’m still thankful for friends and family, good food and good weather, and my dog. 


But somewhere along the years, keeping track of daily gratitude became more of a chore. It was one more thing to do at the end of the day, and in typical child fashion being told to do something made me want to do it even less. I also internalized being told to keep a gratitude journal as a sign that I was ungrateful for what I had. On days where I felt nothing good had happened, it seemed pointless, and as time went by the gaps in my gratitude entries became larger and larger. 


I started keeping track of gratitude more frequently in college. My planner had a designated space for daily gratitude big enough for me to jot down a few things, which I was doing more often. By then, I knew more people who journaled and loved it, and I began to entertain the idea again. 


But I needed this time to be different. Instead of seeing this as a chore, I needed to reframe how I thought about gratitude and appreciating things throughout my day. I started by investing in a cute lavender Moleskine journal. I hoped that if the joy of getting to write in a journal I liked wasn’t enough, the fear of wasting the money I spent on it would motivate me. 


I started by setting aside 15 minutes before bed to journal. This was difficult at first. While in school I had a very flexible bedtime and was usually so exhausted before going to sleep that the last thing I wanted to do was more writing. However, as time progressed, setting time aside not only helped me establish a more consistent nighttime routine, but made me feel calmer and ready for bed which was great for my insomnia. I also started to feel more in control of my day and what I took away from it. Even on particularly challenging days, I could find the positives and channel my energy away from more negativity.  


I started by writing down five things I was grateful for each day, regardless of how good or bad the day was. After the first month of doing this, I noticed that the first few entries were usually more thoughtful while those on the tail end were things I appreciated but didn’t put much thought into. I went from five to three entries per day, with room for more when I felt like it, and I started adding more information. An entry that might have said, “Morning hike with sisters” turned into an entry like, “Today I got outside and went on a morning hike with my sisters. It was great to be active and get some fresh air with them, and we had fun getting coffee after. I felt healthy, active, and it was amazing to spend time with people I love.” I found that writing down the ‘extra’ information gave me more time to reflect and helped me get better at putting my feelings into words. I also felt more grateful! I still have days where I jot down a few things and leave it at that, but the majority of my entries have become more detailed. When I look at past entries, it’s much easier to see what I’m grateful for and what I want to attract more of in my life. 


There are days I forget or feel too tired to recognize any positives, and that’s okay. Instead of forcing myself to express gratitude for things I’m not genuinely grateful for, I grant myself permission to skip an entry. I revisit and add an entry the day after when I’ve gained a new perspective.


I’m a firm believer in the principle of attraction- what you put out, you get back. Since I’ve started keeping a regular gratitude journal, I’ve seen firsthand the transformative power of keeping a regular gratitude journal. I’ve noticed an increase in positive experiences and awareness of the things that I’m grateful for. My overall sense of contentment has shifted and I’ve noticed a reduction in my insomnia symptoms. 


Studies indicate that people who express gratitude more often, whether written or verbally, are less likely to experience common health, digestion, and sleep issues. Over time, these individuals also tend to make healthier nutrition and activity choices. Additionally, expressing gratitude greatly reduces the effects of negativity bias- a psychological theory that suggests that negative experiences have a greater impact on our psychological and emotional states compared to positive experiences of equal strength. By cultivating gratitude, we can actively counteract this bias and create a Unmore positive outlook on life. 


Choosing to seek out the positives in a world that can feel overwhelmingly negative is an empowering act of self- care and resilience that has nourished my mental and physical well-being. Actively acknowledging and appreciating the good in my life has allowed me to experience a heightened sense of gratitude, which has in turn made me a more positive and healthier person mentally, emotionally, and physically.
summary: Gratitude journaling is one of those things that seems easy in theory but difficult in practice, when we have real life demands and stresses to deal with. However, it is during difficult moments that practicing gratitude is the most valuable. Making a conscious effort to seek positivity can train our minds to seek positivity and help us develop a more resilient mindset.

title: From Economically Challenged to Empowered
content:
I started my freshman year in 2018 with virtually no money. My graduation checks had quickly been spent on textbooks, school supplies, and ridiculously expensive yet apparently vital items like a good mattress topper and a functioning laptop (life lesson learned: a quality mattress topper makes all the difference). I quickly got my first on- campus job and immediately implemented what I thought was a solid savings plan. Throughout my four years I had a variety of jobs, from acquisitions aide at my campus library to waitress to Editor-in-Chief of my school’s student newspaper. By 2022, I was hustling my way through senior year with three on- campus jobs, an internship, and a full academic course load. 


Despite being successful on paper, I was struggling to save money. By senior year I was paying for all of my own personal items, groceries, school supplies and fees. The money I made working over the summer was gone by the fall. Expenses like flying from Minnesota home to Colorado once or twice a year for break was a significant financial commitment. Despite working over 60 hours a week, I was making minimum wage and had a cap on my work study hours. While I became a pro at taking advantage of sales and comparing brands, I would still get lightheaded if I spent more than $100 for two to three weeks of groceries. My desperation to save money grew as graduation approached. I didn’t have a job lined up, and a significant ongoing family health crisis continued to greatly threaten my family’s finances. 


Fast forward to three months after graduation. I’d been looking for jobs with little to no success. The money I had saved had vanished. At my lowest, I had a little less than $100 in savings. After pretty seriously considering the benefits of selling my left kidney, I finally landed an amazing job that came with benefits, PTO, and insurance. I was honestly just happy to be receiving a solid weekly paycheck.


I immediately set out to become more financially empowered. While some things had been out of my control as a working student, I knew that my previous savings plan and spending had to change if I was going to successfully save money for grad school and establish a solid financial future for myself. 


I started by creating a better budget. After looking around for inspiration, I settled on a combination of savings methods. I began with a modified 50-30-20 budgeting plan, in which I put the majority of my money towards savings, roughly 30% towards expenses, and around 20% towards lifestyle/ fun expenses. I also use the envelope method. Each week, I withdraw the 20% I set aside in cash and keep it in an envelope, which has made me more conscious of what I spend on nonessentials while also giving myself permission to have fun. I challenge myself to have money left over in the envelope that rolls over to the next week. I also started recording everything in a budgeting planner. While I initially bought a budgeting planner, later I created my own in an old bullet journal. All my planning, saving, spending, and receipts get recorded so I can track my finances and set better long- term goals. 


Now, almost nine months after thinking about the costs and benefits of black market surgery, I’ve saved more money than I thought possible and I’m on track to buying a car and paying for graduate school. I’ve experienced budgeting setbacks and had to fix my plans over time to get where I am now. Getting my finances in check has been one of the most overwhelming and empowering experiences. Being able to take control over money, a concept that seemed unmanageable at best, has given me more confidence and made me more excited about my long- term goals. As daunting as it can seem, my number one piece of advice for anyone just starting to manage their finances is to begin. There’s going to be an adjustment period, but no one gets good at managing their money right away. Just get started, and the rest will fall into place.
summary: In spring 2022, I was set to graduate on time with essentially no money. I didn’t have a job lined up after graduation. A family health emergency was putting my family’s finances in danger. Despite the wealth of resources I took advantage of to find employment and higher education, I felt like I was starting my young adult life miles behind my peers. Here’s what I’ve learned.

title: Exposing The Truth About Credit Scores
content:
Exposing the Truth About Credit Scores

You may have heard the term “credit score” floating around in your adult life, but many feel a lack of confidence in understanding their credit. Credit is framed as an important financial device that can make or break your financial future, but that’s usually where education stops. It appears as a fear factor rather than something to work with. Credit is incredibly important for purchases, but it’s moldable and can be changed with some dedication. Having good credit can assist you with a multitude of things such as lower rent, phone plans, and insurance prices as well as acting as a built-in recommendation when applying for jobs. So how do we get to a place where our credit score is good enough for those perks?


Well, let’s start with defining the basics of credit. Credit is your ability to borrow money or goods and services with the promise of paying for it later. A common example is setting up a payment plan for a big purchase like a laundry machine, car, dishwasher, etc. Everyone has a credit score, which starts upon your first borrowing. For many people, this initial credit is a credit card or a student loan. Your credit starts in the fair score range depending on what/how much you borrow, and the more consistently you pay back on your purchases, the better your credit score will be. The very essential piece of good credit is simply paying back what you borrow.


So, how does credit turn into a credit score? Basically, your borrowing info is provided to and collected by credit reporting agencies. The main three are Equifax, TransUnion, and Experian. These agencies collect this information and use that to create a credit report, which then produces your credit score. A credit report typically includes…

·      Identifying Information (Date of Birth/Social Security Number)

·      Address (Past and Current, Which means there can be multiple listed)

·      Employment (Past and Current)

·      Credit Inquiries (Any time that a company/entity has hard-checked your credit)

·      Tax or Legal Issues (Tax fraud/Criminal History typically)

·      Borrowing History

·      Repayment History

·      Collection Accounts (These are opened due to overdue bills typically)

The information collected in your credit report is then used to determine your credit score. The credit report acts as a way to gauge how much financial risk you pose for lenders, which is turned into your credit score. A higher score means lower risk and a lower score means higher risk.

There are two major types of credit scores, FICO and VantageScore. Most lenders check your FICO score, but typically banking refers to VantageScore. They both use pretty similar methods to score, often leaving just a couple of points difference at any given time. Both are scored on a scale of 300-850, with anything above 661 considered a good score. 661 being just above the midpoint is very achievable for the average person, and it tells lenders that you are more likely to pay the money back. Many things go into this score as we mentioned earlier, but the major things that can change your score are payment history, the amount owed, length of credit history in total, credit mix (do you have many types of credit/many different places you’re borrowing from), and new credits.


The key ways to build credit really revolve around making payments on time. Some people start their credit by becoming an authorized user on another person’s credit account. The benefits of this vary based on how good the other person’s credit is, but this can act as a great way to dip your toes into managing your credit score. Being an authorized user allows you to use money and make payments (build credit), without total responsibility. Ultimately, the account doesn’t belong to you, but you can use it to start your credit journey. It’s also a good idea to start borrowing small amounts through a credit card as an introduction to credit. Many choose to apply for a secure or student credit card, which requires you to place a security deposit in order to avoid the risk for the lender. These cards often have lower limits, allowing users to borrow a lower amount instead of taking a lot and not being able to make payments. Other tips for building credit include paying bills on time and consistently, keeping card balances relatively low, keeping multiple credit cards open even if you don’t use them often, mixing types of credit (not having just a credit card), and regularly checking your credit score.


The number one mistake young adults make when opening credit accounts is missing payments. This is a sure way to chip away at your credit rather than build it up. Another extremely common mistake is applying for many types of credit within a short period of time. When companies look at your credit score and credit report, they will be able to see these applications and other inquiries, which makes it look like you are desperate to get credit. In addition to that, hard inquiries can actually lower your score just because the lender checked. Other common mistakes are, forgetting about closed accounts with balances (think canceled cable with one bill left), not paying off credit card balances, misusing credit cards (taking more than you can pay), and falling for instant approval scams which have insanely high interest rates.


It can take a decently long time to get your credit as high as you want it. It mostly takes patience and dedication, as long as you’re making your payments on time, have faith that your credit score will rise. Hopefully, this article provides a way to look inside the big, scary concept of credit and a way to realize that it’s not super complicated after all. There are many intricacies to managing credit, but as long as you borrow within your means and make your payments, you’ll have a good credit score in no time!
summary: You may have heard the term “credit score” floating around in your adult life, but many feel a lack of confidence in understanding their credit. Credit is framed as an important financial device that can make or break your financial future, but that’s usually where education stops. It appears as a fear factor rather than something to work with. Credit is incredibly important for purchases, but it’s moldable and can be changed with some dedication. Having good credit can assist you with a multitude of things such as lower rent, phone plans, and insurance prices as well as acting as a built-in recommendation when applying for jobs. So how do we get to a place where our credit score is good enough for those perks?

title: Stylish and Sustainable: Eco-Friendly Fashion for a Cool Summer
content:
Summer is officially here! Pools are open, swimsuits are back in stores, and severe weather is sweeping the U.S. From triple digit temperatures in the south and Midwest to tornadoes and hailstorms in the west and southwest, this summer is shaping up to be a record- breaker. In addition to staying hydrated, cool, and using sunscreen, the clothing we wear plays a large role in temperature regulation. We’ve put together a few ways you can stay cool and shop sustainably this summer without breaking the bank.


Great news! Cotton- one of the most popular clothing textiles- is also great at keeping you cool and is sustainable in either its organic or recycled forms. It is also biodegradable. Debating between organic and conventional cotton? Though only 1.4% of cotton worldwide is produced organically, it is grown without chemicals and is grown and harvested using ancestral farming methods, meaning it’s better for the environment and for the people producing it. 


Linen is also a great choice and is made from flax, which requires less water and energy to produce than many other textiles. Flax can grow in poor conditions and can also help replenish polluted soil. Its loose weave allows heat to escape the body and it absorbs moisture well. However, linen does wrinkle easily and can have a divisive texture. For best results, most experts recommend dry cleaning linen fabrics. 


Hemp is very similar to linen, and the weave helps heat escape while wicking moisture away from your body. It requires minimal water and pesticides and has positive effects on the soil it’s grown in. Hemp also grows incredibly fast, and can be machine washed. Besides 100% hemp, there are also several sustainable blends, like hemp bamboo and hemp lyocell.  


Rayon is made from wood pulp, cotton, and other natural fibers like eucalyptus, and is often marketed as being eco-friendly. It is soft, affordable, lightweight, and is found in many textiles. However, rayon has a few drawbacks. Processing the materials used to create rayon requires many harmful chemicals and releases pollutants. If you’re looking for a more sustainable rayon dupe, check out lyocell or sustainable viscose, which is made of the same materials but requires less water to make and produces much fewer pollutants. 


Shopping sustainably doesn’t have to mean spending the big bucks, either. Make no mistake- more sustainably produced textiles are often more expensive than their mass- produced counterparts, but the price reflects the labor that goes into sustainable producing and fairly compensating workers. Check out brands like TAMGA, Wearwell, ABLE, Girlfriend, and Happy Earth, all of which carry a range of affordable and sustainable styles and sizes. 


If you haven’t tried a clothing subscription service yet, here’s your sign! Clothing subscription services like StitchFix allow members to try before they buy, which helps reduce clothing waste. Members benefit from the help of a personal stylist and can choose from different brands (including sustainable ones!) and styles. 


One key aspect of sustainable clothing use is the water and energy we put into maintaining our clothes. Water and energy bills are already high in the summer thanks to air conditioning and keeping our lawns and gardens green and growing. Throw in the fact that we’re sweating more often and have things like bathing suits and beach towels to clean, and your wallet is already feeling lighter. One easy way to save? Pay attention to the washing instructions on your clothing! Not only can most clothes be cleaned in cold water, which reduces energy, but following care instructions helps extend the longevity of your clothing and reduces clothes waste in the long term. Doing full loads of laundry is also more water- efficient compared to multiple small loads. Finally, air drying- especially for items like synthetic fabrics, wool, and delicates- saves both energy and keeps your clothing in better condition for longer. 


Have a cool, sustainable summer!
summary: Looking for affordable ways to beat the summer heat? Embrace eco-friendly fashion for a cool and pocket-friendly summer style. Discover a world of sustainable and stylish options that not only keep you comfortable but also contribute to a greener planet.

title: How Can We Manage Debt?
content:
How Can We Manage Debt?

Being in some sort of financial debt has become incredibly normalized for Americans in adulthood. Most have some student debt from college education, credit card debt, or are paying a mortgage. Debt definitely has an effect on the average person, often causing financial stress and conflict in their daily lives. Some get so overwhelmed that they simply choose to ignore their debt and let it pile up behind closed doors. So, what can we do about this?


Make a plan for paying off your debt: It’s important to decide early that paying off your debt is a priority. Pursuing a debt-free life can grant you some peace of mind, but having a plan can also provide you with some financial security. A common strategy is to start with the smallest debts first. It’s easy to feel like you’re accomplishing more when you’re clearing debts completely off of your list. This can help you to create a rolling effect within your debts, leading you up to your larger challenges.


Track your spending: Try tracking all of your expenses for one month. This will show you exactly what you’re spending your money on, which can be motivating on its own. It shows you specifically how much you’re spending on unnecessary little treats (coffee anyone?) and how much of your income goes towards your inherent living expenses. A few dollars here and there add up at the end of the month and eliminating just a few of those extra costs can go a long way towards chipping at that debt.


Start a budget: Look at your income and list out how much money you’re willing to put into each category. Start with the absolutely necessary things like rent, groceries, and utilities, and then distribute the money left over from your income. A budget helps you decide where you want your money to go and can help you make decisions when presented with expenses. There are plenty of templates out there to help you get started, or you could look into tools like You Need a Budget or Mint.


Check-in with yourself: Starting a budget can seem overwhelming at first. It can be helpful to do regular check-ins regarding your budget. Are you actually following the expenses that you set? Do you need to change the numbers to be more realistic for yourself? It’s important to stick to a budget, but it can also be flexible and tailored completely to you. Having regular check-ins with yourself helps you feel secure in this new territory of tracking expenses. They can also hold you more accountable to your spending goals, keeping this at the forefront of your mind via your check-ins.


Save, save, save: It sounds a little backward, but a good place to start is by getting money in your own bank account. Look into opening a savings account at a bank you already use, that way it’s easy to access, but not tied to your main expenses. Often people feel pressured to use credit cards for emergencies because they don’t have the extra cash laying around, so starting a savings account can prevent you from falling into that trap! You should shoot for having about six months’ worth of income in that separate account. Consider having direct deposit set where some of your paycheck automatically goes into that account to prevent you from cutting the deposit short.


Spend within your lifestyle: It can be tempting to spend more as you earn more, but this leads you right back to square one of living paycheck to paycheck. Try to spend the same amount and save more as your income increases. This method will speed up the growth of your savings and your ability to pay your debt. It can be tempting to make the minimum payment and spend that extra cash somewhere else, but this extends the life of your debt rather than eliminating it. Try not to compare your lifestyle to those on Instagram or even your peers, you want to work for you!


Working on debt can be overwhelming and stressful, but hopefully, our ideas give you a place to start on your journey. Debt can definitely be eliminated through careful consideration and tactics to hold yourself to. Taking the first steps to work through debt is the hardest part, but once you start it becomes part of your routine. You got this!

Some get so overwhelmed that they simply choose to ignore their debt and let it pile up behind closed doors. So, what can we do about this?

title: Empowered Salary Negotiation: An Insider’s View
content:
Every job offer negotiation is like a kitchen remodel, it deserves at least one good counter :)


This is what I tell all my private clients of successful women at all levels evaluating their next career opportunity.


It seems like society hasn’t done enough to support and facilitate women advocating for themselves during the job offer negotiation process. 


And while that is truly unfortunate, it becomes your responsibility to change that for yourself by using your voice. Because if you don’t, you’re leaving money on the table.


The two biggest hurdles to success in job offer negotiation that I see are:

  1. Not negotiating at all and just accept the first offer
  2. Being willing to negotiate but not knowing if you could have asked for more or how to do that


This article is intended to show you that you can negotiate, you should negotiate, and the best practices on how to negotiate. All so that you can maximize your earnings by effectively managing the negotiation conversation.


My name is Aaron Thweatt and I’m an Executive Coach with a specialty of helping women negotiate their salaries. I come to you with this message because I want to start a movement of women advocating for themselves and doing it so well that they can maximize their earnings by using their voices. Developing this skill set is a key facet of owning your future.


I have the ability to help because I spent 11 years in the function of HR known as compensation at four different tech companies, most notably, SpaceX and DoorDash (corporate). This means I determined compensation policies and told recruiters and hiring managers yes or no on how much they could pay thousands of people. I know how the game works and I’m here to help.


Let’s get into it.


A few additional points to empower you to know you can negotiate before I show you how.


The first thing to consider is time.


Let’s say it takes 1 minute to actually say the words to negotiate. And let’s say you switch jobs seven times in your career.


That’s seven minutes to negotiate your entire life’s earnings!


If you don’t negotiate on the first, second, or third job out of school, you’re potentially missing out on the compounding that would come from those conversations. Perhaps by the time your fourth job change rolls around, you finally negotiate. That’s great! But it’s potentially not off of as high of a basis as it could’ve been.


And more importantly, as your career grows, your leverage typically grows exponentially rather than linearly. So how much you can earn with 3 years of experience is nowhere near as high as you can make with 7 to 10 years of experience (side note: This is why sometimes one of the best ways to get a raise in Corporate America is to switch jobs).


But if you haven’t developed the somatic body to have those tough conversations early on and build with each successive job change, then you’re not going to be as equipped to swing for the fences when you have that robust set of career leverage down the line. It really comes down to a conversation: say the right words, get more money.


So start now.


Finally, if you can’t advocate for yourself, how can you advocate on the company’s behalf?


This is actually a paradox. I’ve seen plenty of people not push it on their offer because they are hesitant to ask because they didn’t want to seem like they were going to be a problem. 


They didn’t want to seem like they were ungrateful for the offer. 


They didn’t want to be viewed as greedy.


So they just quietly accepted the offer.


Then, they came in and absolutely crushed it and were the best performer on the team.


I’ve also had hiring managers tell me while we were discussing what to offer a candidate, “I want to see if they negotiate.”


This particular instance was for a role where negotiation was a daily part of the job.


But many jobs rely on you advocating on the company’s behalf even if it’s not sales, finance, legal, or procurement. Suffice it to say, hiring managers are expecting you to negotiate, so it’s not weird.


Hopefully by now, if you’ve been hesitant to negotiate, you can still move forward knowing that you’re supported by these paradigms. Advocating for yourself is a feature, not a bug.


Now let’s get into the fun stuff on HOW to negotiate your next offer.


The first thing is researching market data. There’s actually a growing number of data sources out there, especially with pay transparency laws coming into effect.


If you’re in a technical role, you probably know about levels.fyi.


Of course, salary.com or Glassdoor are ok resources.


But my favorite resource is looking at the job posting at the company (if they have it listed) and similar postings at competitors in states that have pay transparency laws like California, New York, Colorado, etc. This can inform you what the market rate of pay is, depending on the geography.


Typically, they only show the salary range. So it’s important to take note of all this data and craft a narrative about why you fit into the higher end of the range you find (this is one of the many core components of my coaching services that I help clients with if you ever need help).


But it’s important to also consider total compensation, especially if you work at a tech company, or are in sales, finance, or management.


What is total compensation? 


Base salary + bonus + equity = total compensation


To be clear, benefits are not included in the total compensation discussion. They’re important to understand, particularly if the benefits aren’t as good as where you are currently working, or a competing offer that you have.


But don’t ever let someone tell you that the “good” benefits should make up for lower pay. 


We assume benefits are generally the same across companies and industries. So they are par for the course. The real differentiation is in how much you're paid and what the value of your skill set is in the market.


This brings us to the first tactic of actually handling the negotiation. It’s important to understand that the negotiation starts on the first phone call with the Recruiter. 


They will ask you, usually at the end of the phone screen before passing you onto the hiring manager, “What are your salary expectations?”


Most career advice says to state a range at this juncture. That’s not bad per se. 


But because you’re part of the GrasshoppHer community that finds the best practitioners in their respective disciplines, you have access to premium content from an industry insider like myself. So I’m going to show you how to level up your game.


This is where you turn it around and say, “I’m glad we’re discussing this. What is your company’s compensation philosophy for this role?“


The idea here is to elicit more information to have them tell you how they define the compensation ranges for this role. Not just in salary, but also, is there a bonus? What is the bonus target and how is it determined? How much is the new hire equity?


To get you to quote a salary range on the phone screen before you’ve even interviewed to understand the scope of the role and your leverage is the lowest it’s not in your benefit.


Don’t take the bait.


At this juncture, they may just tell you. The answer could look something like this:


“Base salary is $90,000, bonus target is 10% of your salary, and there is equity granted upon hire, and annually based on performance”.


Now you have more clarity. But at this juncture, they’re going to bounce the ball back into your court so you must be ready. Remember the goal here is to punt and not commit to a salary range until you have more information about the role.


Your response could be something like this:


“I appreciate you sharing that. At this juncture, I want to ensure I understand the full scope of the role and how many of my skillsets you will need. I’d like to continue the interview process to get the full picture. What is the next best step to have that conversation?”


If they cannot tell you or don’t know the range yet because the role is new, but they were asking you for your range, that is another example of why it’s best to wait. Their actual range could be much higher than you would have asked for!


There are some alternative strategies to handle other scenarios where they continue to push you for a number. But this should handle the bulk of your situations and this blog post is already very long. Plus, I have more dynamite stuff to tell you.


Now, after the phone screen you go into the interview loop where you’ll do anywhere from 3 to 8 different interview rounds.


Typically money is not discussed this whole time until the very end when there’s an offer.


Before I get into discussing the final offer, I want to expound upon something that you need to clarify early on that’s really going to impact how much you make in this job. In order to make the most amount of money you have to have the best salary range, right? 


And what sets the salary range? 


The level of the job.


As you get further into your career, you’ll be able to quickly assess if the company has leveled the job that you’re interviewing for appropriately. 


If you feel like you’re in a new industry, or you’re earlier in your career, or you’re getting into a new role that would be considered a promotion for you and you don’t know how much the scope increase truly should be, consult people in the industry, peers, or a coach.


Ensuring that you’re interviewing for the proper level of role is a key factor. You have to get the qualitative right before you address the quantitative.


You don’t want to get to the end of an interview loop and they give you an offer that’s way too low for your skill set.


A brief example is:


If you’re interviewing for a Senior Financial Analyst role but you can see either by the way the job description is written or from the interview process that it’s just a regular Financial Analyst, then a discussion about the level is warranted.


There’s potential that an under-leveled role could adversely affect how much you're paid. So ensure you feel good about the scope and level of the role before accepting the offer.


And this next topic is a whole blog post on its own, but I will make reference to the fact that the way that you interview is also the way that you negotiate your offer. 


What do I mean? 


During your interview, you should seek opportunities to find their biggest pain points. Whether it be ones the hiring manager is dealing with themselves, the team, or the company at large. How can you in this role alleviate them? 


Articulate how you can solve those problems better than anyone else and show them your plan for becoming a top performer.


These points will be the ones you reiterate as justification as to why you are worth the investment when you counter later.

After what usually amounts to an intense interview loop, you get the offer!


The recruiter typically calls you and extends the offer verbally. They’re going to ask what you think about it. It’s best to show excitement and gratitude for the opportunity, but be neutral in your response about the compensation. Say something like, “Thank you so much, this is really exciting that we are on the precipice of working together. I’d like to take a few days to consider the offer further. May I have it in writing to review?“


Make sure that you have a few days to review all the components before getting back. Typically, no matter what your level of negotiating experience, I usually have all my clients punt on saying anything that resembles a counter on the verbal offer call. We want to think holistically about all the components, both financially and non-monetary that are important to you in taking this job. So when you do that with amped up emotions of excitement, you’re not thinking with all of your faculties. Limbic responses are not the best for maximizing your value.


So best to chill out and evaluate everything holistically from a place of being calm and centered. And ideally having an expert review the numbers and the strategy to counter properly to ask for more is always helpful.


Now remember how we started our discussion today? It’s time to put that counter into this kitchen remodel. 


This is your opportunity to remember that hiring managers and recruiters are expecting you to negotiate. 


Empower and imbue yourself with the confidence that a corporate badass like yourself is expected to have the ability to manage this conversation. And you can do it.


You’re not being greedy by asking.


So assess the components of the base, the bonus, and equity (if there is any), and come back with an ask that is well-informed based on your research to get to your desired total compensation. A strong narrative about how you can deliver on the known pain points of the team and the company and how excited you are to work there if you can get these numbers is key.


There are more nuances and strategies around the final offer that are possible depending on your unique situation and what things you want to negotiate for.


But this is a solid framework that will get you through the process without making the primary mistakes that many beginners make and sets you up to make a strong ask at the end without painting yourself into a corner early on.


If you have any questions, please connect with me on LinkedIn, DM me @aaronthweatt on all platforms, or email me at aaron@resparkcoaching.com. It would be amazing to be of service to you and help you in your next negotiation.


Here’s to your continued excellence and future success negotiating!


﻿By Aaron Thweatt, CHPC of Respark Coaching
summary: Every job offer negotiation is like a kitchen remodel, it deserves at least one good counter :)

title: Layoffs Now and Then: A Personal Lesson 20 Years in the Making
content:
It was November 2008, 2 months after Lehman Brothers collapsed. My mother had come to check in on my new fancy design job, in my new office and a new city to celebrate my three-month review. I walked out of that review with a big fat termination letter and $0 in severance. The economy had collapsed and interior design was not exactly a priority for our clients. I didn’t know how I was going to make that month’s rent or any month’s rent after that. After a stiff drink (or a few) with friends, I hurried back to my Brooklyn apartment to update my portfolio and get back on the job market. I got a hot tip on a designer, who needed help with her weekly blogs and a couple of projects in Tribeca and, after a series of interviews, I was hired.  Two days after the Christmas holiday party, I was laid off…again. 


After surviving the emotional and financial trauma of two consecutive layoffs, I had the morbid feeling that 2009 was not going to be a good one. I cobbled together a few part-time jobs including 3 days at a baby retail store in Brooklyn, several shifts at a French fine dining restaurant in Manhattan, and 2 evenings tutoring the GED in Queens, but even my extreme schedule juggling and commuting antics were no match for one of the world’s most expensive cities. I reluctantly surrendered my apartment lease and moved myself and my dogs back to my mother’s apartment in Toronto. 


I hit the job-hunting pavement with the ferocity of someone who was trying to justify her three degrees and save her pride. After three months of interviews, the only work I could secure with an undergrad from an Ivy League university, a law degree, as well as a design degree, was serving burgers at a chain restaurant that did not serve alcohol. My tips were very unimpressive. One night a former law school classmate came in with her husband and two children. After a friendly, but rather defeating exchange, I wasn’t really in the mood to clean her children’s mustard drool off the chairs at closing.


So, that was 2008 and 2009. 2010 wasn’t looking so bright and shiny until a call came in for an interview with McKinsey & Company, the world’s most eminent management consulting firm. When I tell you I had applied for hundreds if not thousands of jobs by that point, I am not exaggerating. I made some calls to folks in my network to understand the role and studied my booty off for that interview. By some miracle, I got an offer to start in the Toronto office on April 1st. 


McKinsey changed my life. Initially thinking I would give it a 6-month go, I found myself having trouble thinking of reasons to leave. Where else could I learn valuable business skills at such a fast rate surrounded by brilliant, diverse opinions and people all on a mission to mentor? Nowhere! It is a place that launched a thousand careers: I became an expert in areas like external relations, talent acquisition and diversity, equity and inclusion. I built a family while at McKinsey, left to launch a social impact start-up, and returned when I found myself seeking more career support and financial security. 


But, McKinsey is not immune to the economy. Earlier in the year, we became aware of Project Magnolia, which threatened to be a reorganization that would claim thousands of jobs. And, my role was one of them. Twenty years older and wiser than my first layoff, I had a couple of things going for me. 1. This time around, I had an emergency backup savings fund that will no doubt prove handy. 2. I also had the wherewithal to call a lawyer. I learned that in the U.S. and in Texas in particular, companies are not required to pay you severance. However, with research, I learned that most countries provide layoff packages that account for pay for 2 weeks for every year you’ve worked with the company and they must pay you out for vacation accrued. I also learned that everything is negotiable. Do not sign termination papers without consulting someone who can walk you through your rights and help you negotiate your package. 3. I downloaded all documents that could be useful for future employment negotiation, such as my letter of employment outlining my salary as well as my 401K and Roth allocations. 4. I asked friends and colleagues to serve as my referrals in my future job hunt. 5. Since I did have some time to consider my situation before my layoff, I put together a personal employment plan. I could afford not to work for 6 months, so I would take this rare opportunity to enjoy my family for 3 months (hello Costa Rica!) and then pound the pavement for employment during the second half of my severance. 


I tell this story to serve as inspiration for anyone who is struggling with job and financial security during this uncertain economic landscape. I have now been through two economic downturns and experienced several layoffs, so I can say a few things: the economy will come back and it is extremely painful to struggle to find or maintain work. The process forces you to consider your self-worth, your decisions, your relationships, and your plans for the future. It heightens your anxiety and, even more so, your vulnerability. The past few weeks since my layoff have reopened wounds that I thought I had healed and have forced me to reconsider my priorities. I am someone who has always defined my self-worth by my career. As a professional dancer come lawyer come designer come strategist come social impact entrepreneur, I’m definitely type A and probably a little off on “what matters” in the grand scheme of life. With my mother’s early and unexpected passing, the pandemic, a marriage, two sons, a city move, three house moves, two puppies, and a start-up in three years, I am starting to realize how fast and short life really is. How do I want to enjoy my time? How do I want to serve my community? How do I want to manage my “wealth”? How much of my time do my kiddos, friends, and relationships deserve? Luckily, with the little bit of wiggle room that I have accrued for myself, I have time to be intentional about answering these questions. DM me @grasshoppher or @heathermillernow if you feel me or have thoughts.

The process forces you to consider your self-worth, your decisions, your relationships, and your plans for the future. It heightens your anxiety and, even more so, your vulnerability.

title: My Therapist Prescribed Journaling
content:
I don’t want this be a therapy tell all. I know, nobody cares. But, what I do want to share with anyone who is interested in listening is the unconventional homework my therapist sent my way. She asked me, “What would I do if you woke up tomorrow and everything was perfect?” and challenged me to journal my answers*. 

 

The first thing I thought about was, “Ooh, do you think Amazon has new, cool Moleskine journals? Or, maybe a should treat myself to a reMarkable?”. But, these questions were really distractions from the task at hand about which I was thoroughly confused. I couldn’t wrap my head around the prompt. “What do you mean what would I DO if everything was perfect?” Number one, that’s totally unrealistic. Number two, perfection for me is waking up in a good mood, making sure all of the babies and fur babies in the house are taken care of, and maybe getting to enjoy a good glass of wine on the patio at the end of the day. If I really had to push myself to think about it, a perfect day would be waking up in Isla Holbox, working out, fitting in some self-maintenance like good eating, dying my roots, or guasha-ing my face, being in a relationship with a mature partner, who respects and enjoys me, having a boozy brunch with some friends …and then maybe a glass of wine on the patio at the end of the day.


But, what Paola (as my friends and I refer to my therapist) was really asking was what ensures you’ll wake up in a good mood? What brings you joy, energy and flow? As soon as Paola mentioned flow, I knew what to do. I pulled out my trusty copy of Design Your Life, written by Stanford Design School’s Bill Burnett and Dave Evans to re-familiarize myself with the premise, which is that the same design thinking that is used to build the world can be used to build your career and life. I’ve taught modules on this theory in many corporate settings and the major discovery prompt is to have people recognize and jot down times of the day when they are in flow. This is when the minutes fly by and you haven’t noticed the clock, when you are fully in the zone and focused on the task at hand, or feeling enjoyment and/or energized by the activity. Ok, I got it. Name “my flow”. My turn!



During this time of introspection, I had the fortune of escaping the kids (and most responsibilities) for my annual parents only vacation. As soon as I made it through airport security, my world renewed. I’ve always been someone who thrives during travel. When I was 20, I studied abroad in Paris and really “found myself”. Or maybe, I found the city. The newness of a place’s architecture, its locals’ fashion customs, and the personality of each neighborhood really peaks my senses. I’m fully in discovery mode sniffing out my next meal, art exhibit or shopping experience. If travel is for pleasure, I’m never really ready to come home.


Then I found myself staying up way past my bedtime. Everyone in the house was asleep except moi, of course. I had just finished nightly hour of wrap up work when my friend texted, “Are you awake?”. Normally, I might pretend to ignore the message and force my head to the pillow, but I had been primed by an earlier conversation. A mutual friend called earlier in the day to get some pointe shoe tips and tricks. She had been sewing her daughter’s ribbons all wrong and got a scolding from the ballet mistress. So, I picked up for this friend too. In a minute I forgot how much work I had left to do, what was on my plate tomorrow and how badly I needed sleep. Instead, my friend and I worked through a work deal conundrum, talked about our taxes and some home design decisions she needed to make. Boring to some, but bliss for me!


The next time I was in flow was during a filming segment for work. The whole prep and production reminded me of a past life when I used to style fashion shoots. I curated the furniture on set (aka my living room), made sure my guest was prepped for the interview and lights, camera, action! We put together an awesome video to help women with salary negotiations. In the meantime, I chatted with my guest about his upcoming trip to Mexico City and hooked him up with neighborhood and friend recommendations. I had a blast curating resources. I’ve always loved sharing my learnings, connecting people, and brokering opportunities. It’s why I do what I do at GrasshoppHer.


In sum, I’ve learned that movement, travel, friendship and conversations and curating resources equal flow state for me. I can’t yet tell you how this exercise will change my life (be sure to tune into my next therapy session), but what I can tell you is that I feel some clarity and a lot of relief. Regarding clarity, I feel like I have mindfully worked out my priorities. Of course, I have others. For example, I need to make sure my kids are happy, healthy, and making friends at school. I also need to renew my car registration sticker. But, when things feel off-kilter, I can return to these four flow states like a mantra and realign myself. As for the relief, I have reminded myself why I launched GrasshoppHer and reassured myself that this is what I am supposed to be doing. The life of an entrepreneur is a tough one. The well-being of the company is on your shoulders, you wear many hats and fulfill many roles and you’re not always sure there is a financial reward at the end of the tunnel. That being said, if you’re an entrepreneur, it’s probably because you want to be and you need to remind yourself of that during every hardship. So, as I struggle through start-up life, I can at least say I love it.

title: Authentic Networking: How to Shift Your Mindset
content:
Authentic Networking: How to Shift Your Mindset

             “Networking feels inauthentic.” If you’ve ever found yourself thinking this when trying to expand your network, you’re not alone. People often think of networking as being fake, trying to appeal to people to forward their own careers for no other reason. Some dismiss it simply on the basis of being introverted, thinking that social networking events only work for extroverts. Even so, networking in today’s workspace is considered a necessity. Research shows that having a professional network leads to more (and better) job opportunities, knowledge, innovation, faster career advancement, and more authority. Having those professional relationships can also lead to more satisfaction surrounding work and better quality of work. So how do people successfully network?

             The baseline of networking is about people enjoying the company of other people. Often, you’re united by a common thread, such as your field of work or even the company that you work at. It’s an opportunity to discuss your passions and interests with people who most likely share some of those passions and interests. Instead of thinking about networking as a way to forward your own career or a professional obligation, try and think about it as a way to build genuine relationships with your peers. You may even want to think about it as a way to find connections for your peers instead of yourself. If you talk to someone who’s looking for something specific, like a graphic designer per say, and then you talk to someone later who is a graphic designer, try to connect those two people. They’ll both note that you remembered something about them, and cared enough to connect them even though it didn’t directly benefit you. That could become the basis of a very fruitful professional relationship just by connecting two people you just met.

             This kind of shift in mindset can be helpful for introducing people to the idea of networking, as well as giving them a basis to start with. When entering a networking environment, it’s important to recognize that everyone there has incredible value. People often go into networking events with a closed mind or a specific list of what they’re looking for. It’s important to give each person that you speak to credit, it’s less about their titles or experience and more about forming a relationship with them and expanding your personal network. Listening to and engaging with each person not only looks good, but it helps to form a genuine bond behind the professional relationship. By being attentive during your first meeting, you establish yourself as someone who is genuine and open-minded. This makes them more likely to reach out to you after the event, both with opportunities and just as a peer.

             Even when approaching these events as peer-focused rather than self-focused, it’s important to have specifics ready about how you can help people. These valuable skills are often behind the obvious ones, but these can be incredibly hard to come up with. People often feel powerless in their jobs, this may be due to their position, the time that they’ve spent at that job, or even that they feel underqualified to be marketing themselves. When people believe that they have a lot to offer, they are more comfortable during the networking process. Try not to focus on exclusively the tangible things that you have to offer. Sure, you have some great connections already, or you know how to code, but what about your ability to adapt? Or your gratitude? It’s important to look past what is obvious and objective and glance into your “invisible” traits.

Approach these events with a general idea of what skills you have under your belt and remember those as you’re getting to know people. If you’re unsure about marketing yourself or you feel like bragging about your skills is out of your comfort zone, simply ask, “How can I help you?”. This is a great way to get people to offer up their needs without you having to give out your whole resume. They may not even have an answer for you right at that moment, but it’s an easy way to give out your LinkedIn, email, business card, or preferred method of contact. This also encourages some sort of follow-up after the initial event.

             You survive the dreaded event, what happens next? Everyone is incredibly busy with their personal lives, let alone their professional lives on top of that. Even so, take a few minutes out of your day when you can to make those follow-ups. If you said that you would reach out to someone, try to within the next business week. If you said that you would connect two people, send out their information as soon as you can. It may seem like a mountainous task, but it only takes a couple of minutes to shoot an email, and you’ll feel better once it’s done. Who wants to have 50 to-dos’ hanging over their head? These follow-up contacts solidify the relationships that you cultivated during the networking period and put you in the minds of the people you contacted. An email quite literally puts your conversation in writing, giving it a place to live on the computer can act as a reminder for you and your new contact to work on your relationship.

             Networking can feel like a hassle and an inauthentic way to make connections, but if you change your approach to the event, you may find that these relationships can be incredibly valuable. The true value of networking is human connection, and if you shift the focus from you to your peers, it’ll be easier to facilitate those genuine connections. As long as you do your part, you never know when the benefits will come to you.

title: Is Work-Life Balance Impossible?
content:
Is Work-Life Balance Impossible?

For many in the workforce, it can feel impossible to maintain a healthy work-life balance. Especially now, in the aftermath of the pandemic, many are working from home with little to no separation between their career and their personal life. Having a good work-life balance is often praised for supporting physical, emotional, and mental well-being, but is that even possible in the current age?


I often see online that the framing of work-life balance can be harmful in itself. The mainstream frames it as work versus life, if you want to put more into one you have to take from the other. Compartmentalizing parts of life may be helpful to some but stress-inducing for others. These types of hard boundaries feel unrealistic to me, especially when the lines between work and life are so blurred. I believe that work and life are separate, but they aren’t mutually exclusive. Work is a huge part of our personal lives, and we have to understand that before we can truly begin to work on maintaining boundaries between our jobs and our lives. What you do at work impacts every part of your life, and that impact is inevitable. So how can we frame our work in a positive light and carry that into our personal life?


It's important to be realistic with yourself and how work is going at the current moment. I often find that it’s hard to have a 100% consistent schedule when work tends to ebb and flow. Some nights you may have to spend more time on work and some nights you’ll be completely free to devote time to your other hobbies and interests. Being hard on yourself with a rigid schedule can actually encourage you to not want to do anything in your free time, let alone work when you need to. Having some grace, awareness, and flexibility can go a long way toward maintaining a healthy balance. I know that this goes against the typical scheduling tips that pop up online, but it can be a lot of pressure to adhere to a set schedule every day. It may help you to identify and prioritize the things that are important to you, both at work and at home. Recognizing your values and your deadlines can push you in the direction of your perfect balance.


It may sound cliché, but being on your phone may actually have you working more hours than ever before. Often, our technology at work and at home are connected, creating a lot of space for overlap during both. Phones are especially guilty of keeping us constantly in the loop with what’s going on at work. A Slack notification goes off and I can’t help but read it and then think about it when I’m going about my time at home. There is an expectation on the rise that every employee will be available 24/7 through their phone. This leads to increased stress and lower productivity at work because people are thinking about work all the time. Setting some boundaries surrounding virtual contact can give some much-needed breathing room away from work. This could be as small as vowing to not check your emails at dinner or no work before breakfast just to create some space outside of work. No one should be working all the time, and trying to check your phone less can be a step in that direction.


Something that I personally struggle with is putting the value of myself into my productivity within work. It’s a symptom of the American dream. If I work hard enough and get rich then I’m successful, and if I don’t make it big then I must not be working hard enough. Don’t get me wrong, it’s important to have those kinds of goals within your work, but it’s not all-encompassing. I’ve found that tying my self-worth to my work leads me to push myself further than I can manage. This kind of pressure decreases the quality of work overall rather than pushing you to be better. Peace and satisfaction within your personal life are just as important as professional satisfaction in maintaining happiness. Work and personal aspirations should go hand in hand, rather than stepping on each other’s toes.


A myth forwarded by the professional industry is that working longer hours makes you a better worker. Working more hours shows that you’re dedicated to the job and will advance your career. Studies have actually found that it’s the opposite. Although this is intended to increase productivity, it undermines work-life balance and leads to dissatisfaction in the workplace. This can produce high turnover rates at companies due to employee stress. If you’ve noticed that you procrastinate your work until the deadline is close: you’re not alone. Try and focus on your productivity with shorter deadlines for yourself. Studies have found that if people are given a long time to complete a project, they often think of the task as too large or too far away and procrastinate. If you give yourself a shorter timeline, it forces you to focus on the task at hand. It takes some experimenting to find your personal groove, but this one can help a lot with distributing workload if you tend to have a lot of work at one time. The key is to work smarter rather than longer.


One last thing to consider may be how you can incorporate your personal life into your work life. Having some breaks and encouragement during your workday can boost your morale and create positive associations with working. Find something that motivates you and try to include micro-breaks in your work. I do this with candy, but it could be anything. I set a small goal, like finishing sending five emails or making that phone call that I’ve been dreading, and then after my goal I have a piece of candy. This kind of encouragement seems silly, but it adds some easy relaxation to your workday and encourages you to start your next task. It could also be nice to focus on something else entirely during longer breaks. Call someone you love at your lunch, watch a youtube video during your ten-minute break, or listen to a song you like when going to get water. These small gestures help to make work and life agree, rather than separating them entirely.


Work-life balance isn’t impossible, but it can be incredibly difficult in current times. Remember to think about the ways that work and your personal life overlap and try to capitalize on or minimize where it’ll help you most. This kind of balance is fluid, and it changes along with you, so make sure to do frequent check-ins with yourself about what’s working and what's not. Work and life go hand-in-hand, you got this!
summary: For many in the workforce, it can feel impossible to maintain a healthy work-life balance. Especially now, in the aftermath of the pandemic, many are working from home with little to no separation between their career and their personal life. Having a good work-life balance is often praised for supporting physical, emotional, and mental well-being, but is that even possible in the current age? Let's explore different mindsets and evaluate our ability to achieve a work-life balance.

title: Side Hustles to Use Your Personal Skills
content:
Side Hustles to Use Your Personal Skills

Side Hustles are becoming extremely popular: and for good reason. They are a great way to add an additional stream of income, plus they allow you to explore business opportunities without a ton of commitment! Side hustles are extremely flexible and can be molded to fit your personal skill set entirely. They can help you explore what your personal skills and passions are in a professional setting, while also providing you with a little extra income. Here’s our list of Side hustle ideas to get you started on achieving your personal and monetary goals. 


1: Freelancing

Freelancers provide work for clients on a per-project basis. You can schedule everything to be in your free time, and your work revolves around what you want to do! If you tend to have a creative mind, check out sites like Upwork, 99designs, or Fiverr. These sites pair freelancers specializing in creative fields like graphic design, writing, and editing with clients who need those kinds of work. You can also look at your personal connections and in our GrasshoppHer community. Chances are, someone you know needs some sort of professional labor that fits your interest, you just have to reach out!


2: Resell Unwanted items

Have you decluttered your closet lately? Trying to get rid of your dusty storage bins? Consider selling those loved items that you don’t use anymore. That old tee shirt could earn you an extra dollar! It’s easy to search online and see what a reasonable price for an item is, plus selling online is accessible to a wide audience. Check out sites like Facebook Marketplace, Amazon, eBay, Poshmark, ThreadUp, and Depop to put up your virtual storefront and get to selling! If you happen to enjoy this process, you could also think about reselling thrifted items on these same platforms. This promotes an ethical clothing cycle while enabling you to get paid for your time in addition to the price of the item. 


3: Tutoring/Personal Instruction

Tutors and Personal Instructors are always in demand, no matter where you are. If you have a secret talent or excelled in a course in school, look into tutoring! Your personal network can probably connect you to a child who is struggling in school. You don’t have to be a kid to learn something new though, so don’t be afraid to ask your peers if they’re interested in your lessons. You could also market both virtual and in-person sessions for flexibility in clients. There are plenty of apps and websites to recruit clientele like Skooli, TakeLessons.com, TutorMe, and Wyzant. Share your personal skills and earn a little extra income!


4: Test Apps and Websites

Businesses and developers are always launching new apps and websites that need testing before their official launch. If you have an eye for detail and enjoy exploring new platforms, this hustle is for you. Being a tester involves going through the app or website, pressing all the buttons, and spending a small amount of time exploring everything you can on the platform. It requires very little commitment to add some additional padding to your pockets by the end of the month. Look into matching sites like UserTesting, Enroll, and UTest to get clicking! 


5: Take Online Paid Surveys

Many companies and marketing researchers want to know consumer opinions on products. Taking online surveys is a very low commitment and a simple way to make a little extra cash. Most sites have you sign up for surveys that you’re interested in, and then if you’re selected, you complete the questionnaire. The selection process can be a little picky, so it takes more waiting time than some of the other hustles to get started. The pay is typically based on how much time you spend on the survey. A more in-depth review warrants higher pay. If you like writing and sharing your opinions check out sites like Survey Junkie, SwagBucks, and Branded Surveys to get started!


6: Transcription

Are you a quick typer and have an eye for detail? Transcription may be the ideal side hustle for you. Transcribers receive audio files and have to type out what they hear. This could be anything from phone calls to legal proceedings, so the amount of work varies depending on how much you want to put into it! It’s a simple job but takes a good ear and quick fingers. Check out sites like GoTranscript, TranscribeMe, and Rev to see paid transcription opportunities.


7: Sell Your Craft

If you have a creative hobby, you might look into selling the things that you create for profit. Homemade goods often sell for a good price and can require low labor. This is a great option if you already enjoy making crafts or art! Hobbies can make a great foundation for the side hustle of your dreams, and it’s a good way to turn your passion into income. Most creators set up their storefronts on sites like Esty, Depop, or Shopify. Don’t be afraid to post on your personal social media and reach out to your peers! People are more likely to support a local seller if they know them personally.


Considerations Before You Start the Side Hustle

One or more side hustle options may sound great to you, but there are a few things to consider before you really get started. Adding an additional form of work can quickly become overwhelming, so it’s important to take a realistic look at what’s possible for you.

  • Is this financially viable for me?


You don’t want to drown yourself in high costs with something that you’re doing on the side! It’ll be beneficial to try and keep initial costs low and then invest more later if you feel comfortable in the side hustle. 

  • Can I make this fit into my current schedule?


It’s important to be mindful of your current schedule and time commitments. You don’t want to pick up something additional that will come at a detriment to your other responsibilities. It may be helpful to pick a side hustle that has scheduling flexibility in case something comes up in your personal life/main job. 

  • Does this fit my passions/interests?


Having an additional side hustle on top of typical responsibilities can be exhausting. It’s important that your hustle is something that you enjoy doing and you’re interested in. Enthusiasm surrounding your hustle not only keeps it going but also helps to enrich the time that you spend on the project. 


Side Hustles can act as an amazing sandbox for you to explore your skills and passions within a workspace. They can also give you valuable skills and experiences as a business professional. It might not always feel intuitive or easy, but it can be incredibly beneficial to explore during professional development (plus a little extra cash never hurt).

title: From Burnout to Motivation
content:
Regardless of where you are on your educational, professional, or personal journey, getting and staying motivated can be a huge challenge. We’ve created a list of ways you can stay on track and motivated to achieve your goals, as well as what you can do when you’re feeling burnt out. 


Starting Positive

Before you can start planning, you first have to get into the right mindset. Your beliefs dictate your outcome, so a positive outlook and belief in yourself is the key to beginning to achieve your goals. 


Small Steps

Setting goals for yourself can feel overwhelming and exhausting. Instead of having one large goal, like getting a promotion or nailing a final, break it down into smaller, achievable steps that you can start working on now. Maybe in order to get a good grade on a final, you can start a study group, or go in to meet with your professor weekly with questions. If your overall goal is to get a promotion, the first step could be to do well on an upcoming presentation. How can you improve your presentation? Where can you get feedback?


Ambitious > Basic

Basic goals are key to reaching your overall goal, but you’re more likely to be excited and motivated about working towards something big. Statistically, having and reaching larger goals leads to increased performance and commitment. 


Get support!

If you have support from family, friends, or coworkers, tell them about your goal(s) and what you’re doing to make it happen. Their positive support can help you stay excited about what you’re working towards.


Find a mentor

Getting where you want to be can be difficult without help. Reach out to coworkers, friends, family members, or teachers to see if they can help you figure out what you want to be doing and where you want to be. 


Reward and review

Reward yourself for achieving your small goals, no matter how small they may seem. Even a little step is still progress towards your larger goal, and it’s always worth celebrating your success. Rewarding yourself is also a good way to keep yourself motivated and moving forwards, even if things get difficult or you encounter setbacks.


Every so often, review your goals. If working towards a certain goal is causing you more stress than excitement, it might be worthwhile to re-examine your goal and why you want to reach it. Maybe a goal you set for yourself three months ago no longer applies to what you’re working towards. If your goal no longer works for you, let it go, and create a new one. As you grow and change, your goals will too. 


Burnout is real, and when it hits it’s easy to lose sight of what you’ve been excited about or working towards. Here are some ideas for when you lose motivation:


The ‘why’

Figure out why you have this goal, and why you want to achieve it. Your answer to this question can keep you driven and inspired, even if the road to success gets tough. 


Inspiration

Try to pull inspiration from outside sources. You could read an autobiography or a memoir by someone you admire, or talk to a mentor or someone who supports you and your goals. See if they can help you see things in a new light, or have any ideas or information that can help you get back on track. If you shared your goal with these people when you first got started, they can remind you of your original excitement and drive.


Self- Compassion

When you hit burnout, it’s easy to be hard on yourself and try to push past it. However, trying to push yourself too much will only lead to further loss of motivation and more stress. Instead, treat yourself with the same empathy and compassion you’d give a friend in your same situation, and pay attention to your mental, physical, and emotional health. 


Some easy ways to prioritize yourself when you’re feeling burnt out can be making sure you get enough restful sleep, balancing your time alone and with loved ones, getting physical exercise, eating nutritious meals, staying hydrated, and practicing mindfulness. 


Starting over

It is always okay to start fresh! Sometimes goals change, and there’s nothing wrong with deciding you want to pursue something new. It’s likely that the goals you’ve set in the past and the hard work you put into achieving them will help you move forwards with your new goal. You are not letting yourself or others down by changing direction or goals.
summary: Is it hard to stay motivated? Burnout hitting hard? Check out our list of goal- setting ideas and burnout coping strategies.
